title: Survival Analysis & Propensity Scores in R
text:
Welcome
This book is a hands-on introduction to three closely related tools for analysing health (and other) data in R:
The last chapter combines them. It takes an observational cohort, matches treated and untreated patients on their propensity scores, and then estimates the treatment effect on survival with Kaplan–Meier and Cox models.

 How the chapters fit together. Chapters 1–3 describe and model survival, and Chapter 4 covers three common traps. Chapters 5–6 deal with confounding in observational data. Chapter 7 then uses the Chapter 2–3 methods (dotted arrows) on the matched data. 




Kaplan–Meier curves describe survival over time, and the log-rank test asks whether groups differ.
Cox regression measures how much groups differ (a hazard ratio) and can adjust for other variables.
When treatment wasn’t randomised, treated and untreated patients may differ in ways that also affect survival (confounding). Propensity score matching creates comparable groups first. Then the same KM and Cox methods are used on the matched data.

How to use this book
Each chapter mixes three things:

Concepts. Short explanations of what a method does and why.
R code. Worked examples you can copy, and live exercises you run in the page. Each chapter builds on the last.
Interactive apps. Small simulations that run in your browser. Change the sliders to see how a method behaves. Because the data are simulated, we know the true answer and can see when a method gets it right or wrong.







TipStart here



If you’re new to these topics, read Before you start first. It lists what the book assumes, with short refreshers. It also shows how to set up R and download the course files, and explains what each type of box in the book is for. Unfamiliar terms are defined in the Glossary.


The interactive apps and the R exercises run in your web browser, so you don’t need to install anything to work through the book. Each exercise is a live code box where you write R, run it, and get instant feedback. Chapter 8 (8  Shiny apps for open-ended exploration) describes two extra Shiny apps that you download and run in RStudio.






NoteThe data used in this book




survival::lung: survival of 228 patients with advanced lung cancer (NCCTG). This dataset comes with the survival package and is used in Chapters 1–3. One exercise and Chapter 8 also use survival::veteran, a lung cancer trial. Chapter 4 uses three more datasets from the survival package: mgus2 (a blood condition that can progress to cancer) and the Stanford heart transplant data (jasa and heart).
A simulated observational cohort (Meet the data: a simulated observational cohort). Treatment is given more often to sicker patients, so a naive comparison is misleading. The true treatment effect is known (HR = 0.70). It is used in Chapters 5–7, and you can download the script that creates it.

Chapter 5









NoteRefresher: standard deviation





The standard deviation (SD) measures how spread out values are around their mean. If ages in a group have mean 65 and SD 10, most people are roughly between 55 and 75. In Chapter 5, differences between groups are measured in units of SD (the standardised mean difference), so that age in years and BMI in kg/m² can be compared on the same scale.









NoteRefresher: confidence intervals





A 95% confidence interval (CI) gives a range of plausible values for the true quantity, based on the data. “Median survival 310 days (95% CI 285 to 363)” means the data are consistent with a true median anywhere in roughly that range. Wider intervals mean less certainty, usually because of less data.









NoteRefresher: p-values and hypothesis tests





A test starts from a null hypothesis, usually “no difference”. The p-value is the probability of getting data at least as extreme as yours if the null hypothesis were true. A small p-value (conventionally < 0.05) is evidence against the null.
Three things to remember:

A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
A small p-value doesn’t mean the difference is large or important. Always look at the size of the effect and its CI.
Each test at the 5% level has a 5% chance of a false positive, so running many tests produces false positives. That’s why multiple comparisons are adjusted (Chapter 2).










NoteRefresher: regression and “adjusting for” variables





A regression model relates an outcome to several predictors at once. Each predictor’s coefficient describes its effect holding the other predictors fixed. That’s what “adjusted for age and sex” means: the comparison is between people of the same age and sex. Linear regression does this for a continuous outcome. The Cox model (Chapter 3) does it for survival.









NoteRefresher: odds, odds ratios and logistic regression





If the probability of an event is \(p\), the odds are \(p / (1 - p)\).

Its coefficients are log odds ratios, and exp() turns them into odds ratios. The log-odds (or logit) scale stretches probabilities near 0 and 1 out evenly, which is why Chapter 5 measures distances between propensity scores on that scale.

title: Before you start
text:
The R you need
You should be able to run code in RStudio (or Positron), create objects with <-, and install and load packages. The book also uses a few other features again and again. Here they are in one place.
Data frames and columns. A dataset is a data frame: one row per patient, one column per variable. df$age is the age column, and head(df) shows the first rows.
Factors. A factor is a categorical variable with fixed levels, e.g. sex with levels "Male" and "Female". In models, the first level is the reference group that the other levels are compared with.
Formulas. Almost every modelling function uses a formula, outcome ~ predictors:
glm(treated ~ age + diabetes, data = cohort, family = binomial)  # treated explained by age and diabetes
coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ sex + age, data = lung)               # survival explained by sex and age
survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = lung)                     # ~ 1 means "no groups"
In survival models the outcome is Surv(time, status), which combines follow-up time and whether the event happened (Chapter 1).
The pipe, |>. Read it as “and then”. These two lines do the same thing:
summary(filter(lung, age > 60))
lung |> filter(age > 60) |> summary()
A few dplyr functions. These come from the dplyr package:

mutate() creates or changes a column;
filter() keeps the rows that meet a condition;
select() keeps chosen columns;
group_by() + summarise() calculates summaries for each group.

Getting help. Type ?coxph (or any function name) in the console.

  "MatchIt",    # propensity score matching

  "broom",      # tidy tables of model results

  "shiny"       # only needed for the apps in Chapter 8

# Only needed for the Going further chapters (9-11)

In RStudio, choose File ▸ New Project ▸ New Directory ▸ New Project, and call it something like survival-course. RStudio will look in this folder for any files you load. Save everything for this course there.

title: 1  Time-to-event data and censoring
text:
1.1 What makes survival data special?
This chapter has your first live R exercises: code boxes you can edit and run in the page itself. Section 1.4.1 explains how they work.
In survival analysis (also called time-to-event analysis), the outcome is the time until an event happens. The event might be death, relapse, hospital discharge, injury, or a machine failing. Every observation needs three things:
What makes this kind of data special is censoring. For some people the study ends, or they drop out, before we see their event. All we know is that their event time is longer than the time we observed. The word comes from censorship: like a censor blacking out the rest of a document, the rest of the patient’s story is hidden from us.

title: 1  Time-to-event data and censoring
text:
A clear time origin. When does the clock start? Diagnosis, randomisation, the start of treatment?
A clear event definition.
A time scale. Days, months or years since the origin, or age.








ImportantCensoring is not missing data



A censored observation still tells us something useful. Suppose a patient was last seen alive and event-free after 2.3 years of follow-up. We don’t know when they will die, but we do know they survived at least 2.3 years. Throwing that information away, or treating 2.3 years as if it were the event time, biases the results. Survival methods use exactly what we know, and nothing more.



1.1.1 Types of censoring
All the censoring in this book is right censoring: we know the event happened after a certain time (to the right of it, on a timeline). It has three common causes:

Administrative censoring. The study ends. Patients who joined late are followed for less time.
Loss to follow-up. The patient moves away or withdraws.
Competing events. The patient dies of something else before the event of interest. Strictly, this isn’t censoring at all: someone who has died can never relapse. Treating these deaths as censored is a common mistake (Section 4.2).

Kaplan–Meier and Cox methods assume that censoring is non-informative. At any time, people who are censored must have the same future risk as people who stay under observation. If the sickest patients drop out because they’re sick, this assumption is broken. Chapter 4 has an app that shows what happens then (Section 4.1).

title: 1  Time-to-event data and censoring
section: 1.2 Why not just use the average time, or logistic regression?
text:
1.2 Why not just use the average time, or logistic regression?

The mean observed time is biased downwards, because censored times are shorter than the true event times.
Using the mean among people who had the event throws away the censored people. It is biased towards fast events.
Logistic regression on “died: yes/no” ignores when the event happened. It also mixes up people followed for 1 month with people followed for 5 years.

The app below makes this concrete.

text:
1.4 Survival data in R: the Surv() object
We’ll use the lung dataset from the survival package. It has survival times (in days) for 228 patients with advanced lung cancer.

head(survival::lung)

#>   inst time status age sex ph.ecog ph.karno pat.karno meal.cal wt.loss
#> 1    3  306      2  74   1       1       90       100     1175      NA
#> 2    3  455      2  68   1       0       90        90     1225      15
#> 3    3 1010      1  56   1       0       90        90       NA      15
#> 4    5  210      2  57   1       1       90        60     1150      11
#> 5    1  883      2  60   1       0      100        90       NA       0
#> 6   12 1022      1  74   1       1       50        80      513       0


The important columns are time (days of follow-up) and status. Note that in this dataset status is coded 1 = censored, 2 = dead. R accepts 1/2, but 0/1 or FALSE/TRUE are clearer, so we recode. We also turn sex into a labelled factor.

lung <- survival::lung |>
  mutate(
    status = status - 1,                              # 0 = censored, 1 = died
    sex    = factor(sex, levels = 1:2, labels = c("Male", "Female")),
    time_m = time / 30.44                             # follow-up in months
  )

table(lung$status)        # 63 censored, 165 deaths

#> 
#>   0   1 
#>  63 165


Surv(time, status) combines the two columns into one survival outcome. Censored times are printed with a +:

Surv(lung$time, lung$status)[1:15]

#>  [1]  306   455  1010+  210   883  1022+  310   361   218   166   170   654 
#> [13]  728    71   567


Almost every survival function in R takes a formula with Surv() on the left-hand side, for example:
survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ sex, data = lung)         # Kaplan-Meier, Ch 2
coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ sex + age, data = lung)     # Cox model, Ch 3







NoteGoing further (optional): other forms of Surv()






Surv(start, stop, event): counting-process form. Use it for time-varying covariates and delayed entry (left truncation).
Surv(time, event, type = "interval"): interval-censored data, where you only know the event happened between two visits.

1.4.2 Practice: fill in the blanks
Replace each ______ with the right code, then click Run Code.


















NoteHint 1





status is the column being recoded. Surv() takes the time column first, then the status column.











NoteHint 2

lung$status <- lung$status - 1

1.5 Exercise

1.5.1 Exercise 1.1
These are live exercises: edit the code, click Run Code, and your answer is checked automatically. See Section 1.4.1 if you haven’t used them before.

How many patients in lung have a missing value in ph.ecog (performance score)?
What is the longest follow-up time? Was that patient censored, or did they die? Make this the last line, so it can be checked.
Write down, in one sentence, what the “time origin” and “event” are for lung. (Hint: the help page, ?lung, describes the variables.)



















NoteHint 1





is.na() gives TRUE for each missing value, and sum() counts the TRUEs.











NoteHint 2





which.max(lung$time) gives the row number of the longest time, so lung[which.max(lung$time), c("time", "status")] shows that row.











TipSolution

lung[which.max(lung$time), c("time", "status")]
One patient has a missing ph.ecog. The longest follow-up is 1022 days, and that patient was censored (status = 0): they were still alive at their last follow-up. For part 3, ?lung says time is “survival time in days”, measured from enrolment, and the event is death from any cause.

title: 1  Time-to-event data and censoring
text:
1.6 Summary






ImportantKey points




Survival data record the time until an event. You need a clear time origin, a clear event and a time scale.
A censored observation tells us only that the event happened after the last follow-up. It isn’t missing data. It carries real information.
Ignoring censoring gives the wrong answer: averages of observed times are too low, and yes/no analyses ignore when events happen.
Survival methods assume censoring is non-informative: people who are censored have the same future risk as those still being followed.
In R, Surv(time, status) combines follow-up time and event status (1 = event, 0 = censored). In lung, status must be recoded from 1/2 to 0/1 first.



Answering the question. We can’t just average the follow-up times, because 63 of the 228 patients were censored, so their follow-up times are shorter than their true survival times. We need a method that uses the information in censored patients correctly. That’s the Kaplan–Meier estimator, in the next chapter.

title: 2  Kaplan–Meier curves and the log-rank test
text:
2.1 The idea
The survival function \(S(t)\) is the probability of being event-free beyond time \(t\). Survival curves always start at \(S(0) = 1\) and can only go down.
The Kaplan–Meier (KM) estimator is named after Edward Kaplan and Paul Meier, who published it in 1958 (Kaplan and Meier 1958). Its other name, the product-limit estimator, describes how it works: the curve is the product of the chances of surviving each step. It splits follow-up into steps at each time an event happens. At each event time \(t_j\):

\(n_j\) = number at risk just before \(t_j\). These are people who have not had the event and have not yet been censored.
\(d_j\) = number of events at \(t_j\).
The chance of surviving that step, given you got that far, is \(1 - d_j / n_j\).

Survival to time \(t\) is the product of all the steps so far:
\[
\hat S(t) = \prod_{t_j \le t} \left(1 - \frac{d_j}{n_j}\right)
\]
Censored people count in the risk set until they are censored, and then leave quietly. They never count as an event. This is how KM uses the partial information from censored people.

2.2 Interactive app: Kaplan–Meier by hand
Type survival times separated by commas, and add + to mark a censored time. Edit the data and watch the table and curve update. Try adding a censored time before the first event, or a tie (two events at the same time).

import {kmFit, kmMedian, logrank, makeRandom, nAtRisk, quiz} from "./js/survtools.js"








viewof kmText = Inputs.text({label: "Times (+ = censored)", value: "2, 3+, 4, 4, 6+, 7, 9, 11+, 13, 15+", width: 420})







kmParsed = kmText.split(/[,\s]+/).filter(s => s.length).map(s => ({
  time: parseFloat(s), event: s.trim().endsWith("+") ? 0 : 1
})).filter(d => !isNaN(d.time) && d.time >= 0)
kmHand = kmFit(kmParsed.map(d => d.time), kmParsed.map(d => d.event))
















Inputs.table(kmHand.slice(1).map(r => ({
  "Time t": r.time,
  "At risk (n)": r.nrisk,
  "Events (d)": r.nevent,
  "Censored": r.ncens,
  "Step: 1 − d/n": r.nevent ? `1 − ${r.nevent}/${r.nrisk} = ${(1 - r.nevent / r.nrisk).toFixed(3)}` : "1 (no event)",
  "S(t)": r.surv.toFixed(3)
})), {layout: "auto", rows: 20})







Plot.plot({
  height: 300, y: {domain: [0, 1], label: "Survival probability S(t)", grid: true},
  x: {label: "Time →"},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(kmHand, {x: "time", y: "surv", curve: "step-after", strokeWidth: 2.5, stroke: "#0072B2"}),
    Plot.dot(kmHand.filter(r => r.ncens > 0), {x: "time", y: "surv", symbol: "plus", r: 6, stroke: "#0072B2", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.ruleY([0.5], {stroke: "#D55E00", strokeDasharray: "4,3", strokeOpacity: 0.6}),
    Plot.text([`Median = ${isNaN(kmMedian(kmHand)) ? "not reached" : kmMedian(kmHand)}`],
      {frameAnchor: "top-right", dy: 5, dx: -5, fill: "#D55E00"})
  ]
})













TipCheck your understanding




Why doesn’t the curve drop at a censored time (+)?
After a censored observation, why are the drops at later events bigger?
What happens to the median if the last observation is censored and \(S(t)\) never goes below 0.5?









NoteAnswers





Using the default data (2, 3+, 4, 4, 6+, 7, 9, 11+, 13, 15+):

No drop at a censored time. No event happened there. The censored person just leaves the risk set, so \(d = 0\) and the step factor is \(1 - 0/n = 1\). Look at time 3: \(S(t)\) stays at 0.900.
Bigger drops later. Each censored person who leaves makes the risk set smaller, so each later death is a larger fraction of the people still at risk. The single death at time 2 removes 1/10 of the survival probability (10 at risk). The single death at time 13 removes half of it, because only 2 people are left at risk. This is also why the right-hand end of a KM curve is so uncertain.
Median never reached. The median is the first time \(S(t) \le 0.5\). Here it is 9. If the curve never drops to 0.5, for example because the last observations are censored (try 2, 3+, 4, 6+, 9+, 11+), the median is not reached. R prints NA. Don’t report the last follow-up time instead. Report “not reached”, and give survival at fixed time points or the lower confidence limit for the median if it’s available.

text:
2.3 Kaplan–Meier in R
survfit() fits the KM estimator. ~ 1 means one curve for everyone.

km_all <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = lung)
km_all

#> Call: survfit(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = lung)
#> 
#>        n events median 0.95LCL 0.95UCL
#> [1,] 228    165    310     285     363








TipHow to read this output




n: patients (228). events: deaths (165).
median: the median survival time, 310 days. Half the patients had died by then.
0.95LCL, 0.95UCL: the lower and upper limits of the 95% confidence interval for the median (285 to 363 days).



summary() gives the estimated survival at times you choose. Here we use 180, 365 and 730 days (6 months, 1 year, 2 years):

summary(km_all, times = c(180, 365, 730))

#> Call: survfit(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = lung)
#> 
#>  time n.risk n.event survival std.err lower 95% CI upper 95% CI
#>   180    160      63    0.722  0.0298       0.6655        0.783
#>   365     65      58    0.409  0.0358       0.3447        0.486
#>   730     13      38    0.116  0.0283       0.0716        0.187








TipHow to read this output



One row per chosen time:

n.risk: patients still alive and in follow-up at that time.
n.event: deaths since the previous time shown.
survival: the estimated proportion still alive, \(\hat S(t)\).
lower/upper 95% CI: its confidence interval. (std.err is the standard error, which you rarely need.)



So about 41% of patients (95% CI 34%–49%) were still alive at one year.

2.3.1 Plotting with ggsurvfit
The ggsurvfit package makes good KM plots that work with ggplot2. Use survfit2() instead of survfit(). It is identical, but it remembers the data and variable labels for plotting.

survfit2(Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = lung) |>
  ggsurvfit(linewidth = 1) +
  add_confidence_interval() +
  add_censor_mark(size = 2, alpha = 0.6) +
  add_quantile(y_value = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  add_risktable() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1000, 250)) +
  labs(x = "Days since enrolment", y = "Overall survival probability")







Figure 2.1: Overall Kaplan–Meier curve for the lung cancer data.





The risk table under the plot shows how many patients are still being followed. Always include it. The right-hand end of a KM curve is usually based on very few people, so read it with caution.

title: 2  Kaplan–Meier curves and the log-rank test
text:
2.4 Comparing groups
Put a grouping variable on the right-hand side of the formula:

km_sex <- survfit2(Surv(time, status) ~ sex, data = lung)
km_sex

#> Call: survfit(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ sex, data = lung)
#> 
#>              n events median 0.95LCL 0.95UCL
#> sex=Male   138    112    270     212     310
#> sex=Female  90     53    426     348     550



km_sex |>
  ggsurvfit(linewidth = 1) +
  add_confidence_interval() +
  add_risktable(risktable_stats = "n.risk") +
  add_pvalue(location = "annotation", x = 750) +
  scale_ggsurvfit() +
  labs(x = "Days since enrolment")







Figure 2.2: Kaplan–Meier curves by sex.





The women’s curve stays above the men’s: at every point in time, a higher proportion of women were still alive. Is that difference bigger than we’d expect by chance? Before answering that, we need one new idea.

2.4.1 A first look at the hazard
So far we’ve described survival as the proportion still alive at each time. Another way to describe it is the hazard: the risk of the event right now, for someone who has survived so far.






NoteThe hazard in plain words



Imagine 100 patients are still alive at the start of month 6, and 5 of them die during month 6. The hazard in month 6 is roughly 5 per 100 per month: the death rate among the people still at risk.

The survival curve answers: what proportion are still alive at time t?
The hazard answers: among those still alive, how fast are the events happening right now?

A hazard ratio (HR) compares the hazards of two groups. For example, HR = 0.6 for treatment B vs treatment A means that, at any moment, patients on B are dying at 60% of the rate of patients on A. HR = 1 means no difference.
Chapter 3 covers hazards and hazard ratios properly. For now, “hazard ≈ death rate among those still alive” is all you need.




2.4.2 The log-rank test
The log-rank test asks whether the survival curves are the same. At every time a death occurs, it compares the number of deaths in each group with the number we’d expect if both groups had the same hazard. Then it adds up the differences over all those times.

survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ sex, data = lung)

#> Call:
#> survdiff(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ sex, data = lung)
#> 
#>              N Observed Expected (O-E)^2/E (O-E)^2/V
#> sex=Male   138      112     91.6      4.55      10.3
#> sex=Female  90       53     73.4      5.68      10.3
#> 
#>  Chisq= 10.3  on 1 degrees of freedom, p= 0.001








TipHow to read this output




N: patients in each group.
Observed: deaths that actually happened in each group.
Expected: deaths we’d expect in each group if men and women had the same hazard.
(O-E)^2/E and (O-E)^2/V: intermediate steps in the calculation. You can ignore them.
Chisq … p: the test result. This is the line you report.



Men had 112 deaths when about 91.6 were expected. Women had 53 when about 73.4 were expected. Men died more often than expected and women less often. The test gives \(\chi^2 = 10.3\) on 1 degree of freedom, \(p = 0.001\), so there is strong evidence that survival differed by sex.






WarningWhat the log-rank test can’t do




It gives a p-value only. It doesn’t say how big the difference is. For that we need a hazard ratio (Chapter 3).
It works best when one group’s hazard is a constant multiple of the other’s. If the curves cross, it can miss a real difference.
It does not adjust for other variables. In observational data, a difference in KM curves may be due to confounding (Chapters 5–7).





2.4.3 Practice: fill in the blanks
This is a live exercise: edit the code, click Run Code, and your answer is checked automatically. See Section 1.4.1 if you haven’t used one before.
Do patients aged 70 or over survive less long than younger patients? Replace each ______ with the right code, then click Run Code.


















NoteHint 1





The new column is called old, so that is the grouping variable on the right of each ~.











NoteHint 2





The age cut-off is 70. Time in lung is measured in days, so one year is 365.











TipSolution





lung$old <- lung$age >= 70

fit <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ old, data = lung)
print(fit)
summary(fit, times = 365)
survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ old, data = lung)
Median survival was 283 days for patients aged 70 or over (old=TRUE) and 340 days for younger patients. At one year, about 30% of the older group and 45% of the younger group were still alive. The difference is just significant: log-rank \(\chi^2 = 4.0\) on 1 degree of freedom, p = 0.04.

text:
2.6 Comparing more than two groups
With three or more groups, survdiff() gives an omnibus test. Its null hypothesis is that all the survival curves are the same, so a small p-value tells you that at least one group differs, but not which one.
The lung data record each patient’s ECOG performance status, a score of how well they manage daily activities (0 = fully active, higher = more impaired). Only one patient scored 3, so we combine scores of 2 and 3 into “2+”:

lung <- lung |>
  mutate(ecog = factor(pmin(ph.ecog, 2), levels = 0:2,
                       labels = c("0 (active)", "1", "2+")))

survfit2(Surv(time, status) ~ ecog, data = lung)     # medians by group

#> Call: survfit(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ ecog, data = lung)
#> 
#>    1 observation deleted due to missingness 
#>                   n events median 0.95LCL 0.95UCL
#> ecog=0 (active)  63     37    394     348     574
#> ecog=1          113     82    306     268     429
#> ecog=2+          51     45    183     153     288



survfit2(Surv(time, status) ~ ecog, data = lung) |>
  ggsurvfit(linewidth = 1) +
  add_risktable(risktable_stats = "n.risk") +
  scale_ggsurvfit() +
  labs(x = "Days since enrolment")







Figure 2.3: Kaplan–Meier curves by ECOG performance status.





Median survival falls from 394 days (ECOG 0) to 306 (ECOG 1) and 183 (ECOG 2+). (One patient has no ECOG score, so they are left out.) The omnibus log-rank test:

survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ ecog, data = lung)

#> Call:
#> survdiff(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ ecog, data = lung)
#> 
#> n=227, 1 observation deleted due to missingness.
#> 
#>                   N Observed Expected (O-E)^2/E (O-E)^2/V
#> ecog=0 (active)  63       37     54.2    5.4331    8.2119
#> ecog=1          113       82     83.5    0.0279    0.0573
#> ecog=2+          51       45     26.3   13.2582   15.9641
#> 
#>  Chisq= 19  on 2 degrees of freedom, p= 8e-05


The omnibus test is clear (\(\chi^2 = 19.0\) on 2 degrees of freedom, \(p < 0.001\)). To find out which groups differ, compare each pair of groups. With three groups there are three pairs. Running several tests raises the chance of at least one false positive above 5%, so the p-values are adjusted for multiple testing. The Holm method is a good default. pairwise_survdiff() from the survminer package does all of this:

library(survminer)
pairwise_survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ ecog, data = lung,
                  p.adjust.method = "holm")

#> 
#>  Pairwise comparisons using Log-Rank test 
#> 
#> data:  lung and ecog 
#> 
#>    0 (active) 1     
#> 1  0.0630     -     
#> 2+ 9e-05      0.0052
#> 
#> P value adjustment method: holm








TipHow to read this output



Each number is the Holm-adjusted p-value for one pair of groups. Find a row and a column, e.g. 2+ (row) vs 0 (active) (column), adjusted p = 0.00009.
Always set p.adjust.method. If you leave it out, pairwise_survdiff() uses a less strict adjustment (Benjamini–Hochberg), and you’ll get smaller p-values than these.


Patients with ECOG 2+ had worse survival than both ECOG 0 (adjusted p < 0.001) and ECOG 1 (adjusted p = 0.005). The difference between ECOG 0 and 1 is not significant after adjustment (p = 0.06).
To report how big the differences between groups are (hazard ratios), or to test for a steady trend across ordered groups like these, you need a Cox model. See Section 3.4 in the next chapter.







NoteGoing further (optional): what pairwise_survdiff() does, and Holm vs BH





For each pair of groups, pairwise_survdiff() keeps only the patients in those two groups and runs an ordinary two-group survdiff(). Then it adjusts the p-values. The short function below does the same thing step by step. It’s in pairwise_logrank.R if you want it.

# Copyright (c) 2026 Tom Goodale. SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
# pairwise_logrank() ---------------------------------------------------------
#
# Follow-up comparisons after an omnibus log-rank test with 3+ groups.
# Runs a two-group log-rank test (survdiff) for every pair of groups, using
# only the patients in those two groups, and adjusts the p-values for
# multiple testing (Holm by default; see ?p.adjust for other methods).
#
#   formula : Surv(time, status) ~ group   (one grouping variable)
#   data    : a data frame
#
# Returns one row per pair: the two groups, n, chi-square, raw p, adjusted p.

pairwise_logrank <- function(formula, data, p.adjust.method = "holm") {
  grp <- all.vars(formula)[length(all.vars(formula))]   # the grouping variable
  levs <- levels(factor(data[[grp]]))
  pairs <- combn(levs, 2, simplify = FALSE)

  res <- do.call(rbind, lapply(pairs, function(pr) {
    sub <- data[!is.na(data[[grp]]) & data[[grp]] %in% pr, ]
    sub[[grp]] <- droplevels(factor(sub[[grp]]))
    lr <- survival::survdiff(formula, data = sub)
    data.frame(group1 = pr[1], group2 = pr[2], n = sum(lr$n),
               chisq  = lr$chisq,
               p      = pchisq(lr$chisq, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE))
  }))

  res$p_adj <- p.adjust(res$p, method = p.adjust.method)
  res
}


pairwise_logrank(Surv(time, status) ~ ecog, data = lung)

#>       group1 group2   n     chisq            p        p_adj
#> 1 0 (active)      1 176  3.456831 6.299095e-02 6.299095e-02
#> 2 0 (active)     2+ 114 17.418509 2.998914e-05 8.996742e-05
#> 3          1     2+ 164  9.084970 2.577187e-03 5.154373e-03


The p_adj column matches pairwise_survdiff().

Holm (and Bonferroni) control the family-wise error rate: the chance of making any false-positive claim. Holm is always at least as powerful as Bonferroni.
Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) controls the false discovery rate: the expected proportion of false positives among the comparisons you call significant. It’s less strict, so its adjusted p-values are smaller.





Good practice. Plan your comparisons before you see the data: you often don’t need every pair. (“Each dose vs placebo” is 3 comparisons for 4 groups, not 6.) Say which adjustment you used, and report survival estimates such as medians for each group, not just p-values. A methods sentence might read: “Survival was compared between ECOG groups using the log-rank test, followed by pairwise log-rank tests with Holm’s correction, using the survival (Therneau 2024) and survminer (Kassambara et al. 2021) packages in R.” The references come from citation("survival") and citation("survminer").

2.8 Exercise

2.8.1 Exercise 2.1
The veteran dataset, also in the survival package, comes from a lung cancer trial. celltype records the type of tumour: squamous, smallcell, adeno or large. Its status is already coded 0/1. The exercise has two parts, each checked separately. The packages it needs load the first time you click Run Code, so the first run takes a little longer.

Part 1: KM curves and medians
Draw KM curves by celltype, with a risk table. Then show the median survival in each group (make that the last line).


















NoteHint 1





These are the same functions used for ECOG in Section 2.6: survfit2() with ~ celltype and data = veteran, then ggsurvfit() and add_risktable().











NoteHint 2





Save the fit, e.g. fit <- survfit2(...). Printing fit shows the medians.











TipSolution





fit <- survfit2(Surv(time, status) ~ celltype, data = veteran)
fit |>
  ggsurvfit() +
  add_risktable(risktable_stats = "n.risk") +
  scale_ggsurvfit() +
  labs(x = "Days")
fit
Median survival was 118 days (squamous), 51 (small cell), 51 (adeno) and 156 (large). Small cell and adeno tumours have much shorter survival.









Part 2: log-rank and pairwise tests
Carry out a log-rank test across the four cell types. How many degrees of freedom does it have, and what is its null hypothesis? Then follow it up with Holm-adjusted pairwise comparisons (make that the last line). Which cell types differ?


















NoteHint 1





These are the same functions used for ECOG in Section 2.6: survdiff(), then pairwise_survdiff(). Use data = veteran and ~ celltype.











NoteHint 2





pairwise_survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ celltype, data = veteran,
                  p.adjust.method = ______)











TipSolution





survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ celltype, data = veteran)
pairwise_survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ celltype, data = veteran,
                  p.adjust.method = "holm")
The omnibus test has 3 degrees of freedom (4 groups − 1). Its null hypothesis is that all four curves are identical, and it is clearly rejected (\(\chi^2 = 25.4\), \(p < 0.001\)). The pairwise tests show two clusters: squamous and large cell have similar survival (adjusted p = 0.73), as do small cell and adeno (adjusted p = 0.76). Every comparison between the clusters is significant.

text:
2.9 Summary






ImportantKey points




The KM estimator multiplies together the chances of surviving each event time: \(1 - d/n\). A censored patient leaves the risk set without causing a drop.
Report KM curves with a risk table, plus median survival (or ‘not reached’) and survival at chosen times, each with a 95% CI.
The hazard is the event rate among people still at risk. A hazard ratio compares two groups’ hazards.
The log-rank test checks whether survival curves differ. It gives only a p-value, works best when the hazard ratio is constant, and doesn’t adjust for other variables.
With three or more groups, follow a significant omnibus test with pairwise tests adjusted for multiple testing (e.g. Holm). Always set p.adjust.method.



Answering the question. Yes. Median survival was 426 days for women and 270 days for men. One year after enrolment, about 53% of women and 34% of men were still alive. The log-rank test gave p = 0.001. How much lower women’s risk was, and whether that holds after accounting for age and fitness, is the next chapter’s question.

title: 3  Cox proportional hazards regression
text:
3.1 Hazards and hazard ratios
You met the hazard informally in Section 2.4.1: the death rate among people who are still alive. More precisely, the hazard \(h(t)\) is the instantaneous rate of the event at time \(t\), among people still event-free just before \(t\). Think of it as “the risk right now, given you’ve made it this far”. It is a rate, not a probability, so it can be bigger than 1.
The log-rank test (Chapter 2) can tell us whether two groups differ. The Cox model goes further. It tells us by how much (as a hazard ratio), and it can include several variables at once, so each effect is adjusted for the others.
The Cox model says that each person’s hazard is a shared baseline hazard \(h_0(t)\) multiplied by a factor that depends on their covariates:
\[
h(t \mid x) = h_0(t)\, \exp(\beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \dots)
\]

\(\exp(\beta_k)\) is a hazard ratio (HR). It is the multiplicative change in the hazard for a one-unit increase in \(x_k\), holding the other covariates fixed.
HR = 1 means no association. HR < 1 means lower hazard (protective). HR > 1 means higher hazard.
\(h_0(t)\) is never estimated or assumed to have any shape. This is why the Cox model is called semi-parametric, and why it is so widely used.







ImportantThe key assumption: proportional hazards (PH)



The HR is assumed to be constant over time. If women have 0.6 times the hazard of men at 1 month, they also have 0.6 times the hazard at 2 years. The hazards can rise and fall freely over time, but they have to rise and fall together.


A common misinterpretation: “HR = 0.6” does not mean “40% fewer people die”, or “people live 40% longer”. It means the rate of death at any moment is 40% lower. The effect on the proportion surviving at time \(t\) depends on the baseline hazard, and you can see it by plotting survival curves (see Section 3.7).

section: 3.3 Fitting a Cox model in R
text:
3.3 Fitting a Cox model in R

3.3.1 One covariate

cox_sex <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ sex, data = lung)
summary(cox_sex)

#> Call:
#> coxph(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ sex, data = lung)
#> 
#>   n= 228, number of events= 165 
#> 
#>              coef exp(coef) se(coef)      z Pr(>|z|)   
#> sexFemale -0.5310    0.5880   0.1672 -3.176  0.00149 **
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#>           exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95
#> sexFemale     0.588      1.701    0.4237     0.816
#> 
#> Concordance= 0.579  (se = 0.021 )
#> Likelihood ratio test= 10.63  on 1 df,   p=0.001
#> Wald test            = 10.09  on 1 df,   p=0.001
#> Score (logrank) test = 10.33  on 1 df,   p=0.001








TipHow to read this output



The numbers that matter are the HR, its confidence interval and its p-value:

n, number of events: patients and deaths used in the model.
sexFemale: the effect of being female, compared with the reference group (male).
exp(coef) = HR = 0.59. At any time, women had about 41% lower hazard of death than men.
lower .95, upper .95: the 95% CI for the HR, 0.42 to 0.82.
Pr(>|z|): the p-value, 0.0015.
coef (\(-0.531\)) is the log of the HR. It’s the scale R works on, but you report exp(coef). You can ignore se(coef), z and exp(-coef) for now.
The three tests at the bottom (likelihood ratio, Wald, score) all test whether the model explains anything. They usually agree. The score (log-rank) test is the log-rank test from Chapter 2.
Concordance measures how well the model predicts. See the optional box at the end of the chapter.




From a hazard ratio to a percentage
The percentage change in the hazard is always \((\text{HR} - 1) \times 100\%\):



HR
Percentage change
In words




0.59
\((0.59 - 1) \times 100 = -41\%\)
41% lower hazard


1.00
0%
no difference


1.50
+50%
50% higher hazard


2.50
+150%
150% higher hazard, or “2.5 times the hazard”



So when HR < 1, the reduction is \(1 - \text{HR}\), and when HR > 1, the increase is \(\text{HR} - 1\). Three things to watch:

Use the HR (exp(coef)), not the coefficient (coef). The coefficient is the log HR. Here \(\hat\beta = -0.531\), which is not a 53% reduction.
It isn’t symmetric when you flip the comparison. Women vs men is HR = 0.59, but men vs women is \(1/0.59 = 1.70\): men have a 70% higher hazard, not 41% higher. Both describe the same data. R prints this reverse HR in the exp(-coef) column of summary(). Pick the comparison that matches your research question, and describe it in that direction.
Convert the CI the same way. A 95% CI of 0.42 to 0.82 means a reduction of between 18% and 58%.

And remember, it’s the hazard (the instantaneous rate) that is 41% lower. That isn’t the same as 41% fewer deaths (see the common misinterpretation at the start of this chapter).



3.3.2 Several covariates
Now add age and ECOG performance status (0 = fully active, higher = more impaired). Only one patient has ECOG = 3, so we group it with 2 to avoid an unstable estimate.

lung <- lung |>
  mutate(ecog = factor(pmin(ph.ecog, 2), levels = 0:2,
                       labels = c("0 (active)", "1", "2+")))

cox_multi <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ sex + age + ecog, data = lung)
cox_multi

#> Call:
#> coxph(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ sex + age + ecog, data = lung)
#> 
#>                coef exp(coef)  se(coef)      z       p
#> sexFemale -0.551322  0.576188  0.167987 -3.282 0.00103
#> age        0.011031  1.011092  0.009297  1.186 0.23544
#> ecog1      0.409461  1.506006  0.199596  2.051 0.04022
#> ecog2+     0.915752  2.498654  0.227042  4.033 5.5e-05
#> 
#> Likelihood ratio test=30.08  on 4 df, p=4.704e-06
#> n= 227, number of events= 164 
#>    (1 observation deleted due to missingness)


broom::tidy() gives a tidy table with hazard ratios and CIs:

tidy(cox_multi, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)

#> # A tibble: 4 x 7
#>   term      estimate std.error statistic   p.value conf.low conf.high
#>   <chr>        <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 sexFemale    0.576   0.168       -3.28 0.00103      0.415     0.801
#> 2 age          1.01    0.00930      1.19 0.235        0.993     1.03 
#> 3 ecog1        1.51    0.200        2.05 0.0402       1.02      2.23 
#> 4 ecog2+       2.50    0.227        4.03 0.0000550    1.60      3.90


exponentiate = TRUE converts the coefficients to hazard ratios (estimate), and conf.int = TRUE adds their confidence intervals (conf.low, conf.high).
Interpretation, each holding the other variables constant:

Sex: women have about 0.58 times the hazard of men.
Age: HR = 1.011 per year. Per-year HRs look tiny, so report them per 10 years: \(1.011^{10} \approx 1.12\), a 12% higher hazard per decade (not statistically significant here).
ECOG: compared with ECOG 0, ECOG 1 has HR ≈ 1.5 and ECOG 2+ has HR ≈ 2.5.

To get the HR per 10 years directly in R, use exp(10 * coef(cox_multi)["age"]), or rescale age before fitting (mutate(age10 = age / 10)).


3.3.3 A forest plot


Show the plotting code
tidy(cox_multi, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  mutate(term = recode(term, sexFemale = "Female (vs male)",
                       age = "Age (per year)",
                       ecog1 = "ECOG 1 (vs 0)", `ecog2+` = "ECOG 2+ (vs 0)")) |>
  mutate(term = factor(term, levels = rev(term))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = estimate, y = term)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high), width = 0.15, orientation = "y") +
  geom_point(size = 3, colour = "#0072B2") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Hazard ratio (log scale)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








Figure 3.1: Hazard ratios (95% CI) from the multivariable Cox model.

title: 3  Cox proportional hazards regression
text:
3.4 Comparing three or more groups
In Chapter 2 (Section 2.6), the log-rank test showed that survival differed between the three ECOG groups, and pairwise tests showed which groups differed. A Cox model adds how much they differ. Put the group in as a factor:

coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ ecog, data = lung) |>
  tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)

#> # A tibble: 2 x 7
#>   term   estimate std.error statistic   p.value conf.low conf.high
#>   <chr>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 ecog1      1.45     0.199      1.85 0.0638       0.979      2.13
#> 2 ecog2+     2.54     0.223      4.17 0.0000311    1.64       3.93


Each HR compares one group with the reference group, the first level of the factor: here ECOG 0. Patients with ECOG 1 had about 1.45 times the hazard of death of ECOG 0 patients (95% CI 0.98–2.13), and patients with ECOG 2+ about 2.5 times (1.64–3.93). These are unadjusted HRs. The model in the previous section gave similar values after adjusting for sex and age.
R uses the first level of the factor as the reference. To compare against a different group, use relevel(), e.g. mutate(ecog = relevel(ecog, ref = "1")).

3.4.1 Ordered groups: a test for trend
When the groups have a natural order (age bands, tumour grade, ECOG score), the usual question is whether risk rises steadily across them. A test for trend puts all the evidence into this single question, so it is more powerful than the omnibus log-rank test. To do it, give the ordered groups scores 1, 2, 3, … and fit a Cox model with the score as a number. Here are three age bands in lung:

lung <- lung |>
  mutate(age_grp = cut(age, c(0, 60, 70, Inf), right = FALSE,
                       labels = c("<60", "60-69", "70+")))

survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ age_grp, data = lung)        # omnibus log-rank test

#> Call:
#> survdiff(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ age_grp, data = lung)
#> 
#>                N Observed Expected (O-E)^2/E (O-E)^2/V
#> age_grp=<60   83       56     64.6    1.1357     1.877
#> age_grp=60-69 89       63     65.0    0.0616     0.103
#> age_grp=70+   56       46     35.4    3.1492     4.049
#> 
#>  Chisq= 4.4  on 2 degrees of freedom, p= 0.1

trend <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ as.numeric(age_grp), data = lung)
summary(trend)$sctest                                       # test for trend

#>       test         df     pvalue 
#> 3.87513844 1.00000000 0.04900627


The omnibus test is not significant (\(p = 0.11\)), but the trend test is (\(p = 0.049\)). The omnibus test spreads its power across every possible pattern of differences. The trend test looks only for a steady increase, which is the pattern you’d expect for age. (sctest is the score test. For a single score variable, it is the log-rank test for trend.)







NoteGoing further (optional): every pairwise hazard ratio





The emmeans package gives HRs (with adjusted CIs) for every pair of groups: emmeans::emmeans(model, pairwise ~ ecog, type = "response").

title: 3  Cox proportional hazards regression
text:
3.5 Checking the proportional hazards assumption
cox.zph() tests whether each covariate’s effect changes over time, using scaled Schoenfeld residuals. A small p-value suggests the HR is not constant.

zph <- cox.zph(cox_multi)
zph

#>        chisq df    p
#> sex     2.54  1 0.11
#> age     0.20  1 0.65
#> ecog    3.04  2 0.22
#> GLOBAL  5.24  4 0.26








TipHow to read this output



One row per variable, plus GLOBAL for the whole model. Look at the p column. A small p-value (e.g. < 0.05) suggests that variable’s HR changes over time. (chisq and df are the test statistic and its degrees of freedom.)


None of the tests is significant, so we have no strong evidence against PH. Always look at the plots too. The tests have low power in small datasets and are “too sensitive” in big ones. Each plot shows the estimated log-HR over time. Under PH, the smooth curve should be roughly horizontal.

par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(zph, resid = FALSE, lwd = 2)







Figure 3.2: Scaled Schoenfeld residuals. Flat smooth lines are consistent with proportional hazards.











NoteWhat to do if PH fails




Stratify on that variable: coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ treat + strata(site)). Each stratum gets its own baseline hazard. The cost is that you get no HR for the stratification variable.
Split follow-up time and estimate a separate HR for each period (survSplit()), e.g. an HR for 0–6 months and another for after 6 months. There’s a worked example in Section 3.6.
Report a different effect measure, such as survival differences at fixed times, or the restricted mean survival time (RMST) (see Section 7.5).

More advanced options include time-varying coefficients (tt() in coxph()).
For more, including worked examples of tt(), the RMST and accelerated failure time models, see Chapter 10.









NoteGoing further (optional): is the effect of age a straight line?





A Cox model assumes each continuous covariate has a linear effect on the log-hazard. For example, each extra year of age multiplies the hazard by the same amount. A quick check is to fit a flexible curve (a penalised spline) and test whether it’s needed:

coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ sex + pspline(age, df = 3) + ecog, data = lung)

#> Call:
#> coxph(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ sex + pspline(age, df = 3) + 
#>     ecog, data = lung)
#> 
#>                               coef se(coef)      se2    Chisq   DF       p
#> sexFemale                 -0.55428  0.16845  0.16824 10.82788 1.00   0.001
#> pspline(age, df = 3), lin  0.01106  0.00918  0.00918  1.45168 1.00   0.228
#> pspline(age, df = 3), non                             2.10772 2.09   0.367
#> ecog1                      0.40407  0.20136  0.20071  4.02686 1.00   0.045
#> ecog2+                     0.92278  0.22889  0.22816 16.25345 1.00 5.5e-05
#> 
#> Iterations: 4 outer, 12 Newton-Raphson
#>      Theta= 0.863 
#> Degrees of freedom for terms= 1.0 3.1 2.0 
#> Likelihood ratio test=33  on 6.07 df, p=1e-05
#> n= 227, number of events= 164 
#>    (1 observation deleted due to missingness)


The nonlin row tests departure from a straight line. Here it is not significant, so a linear age term is reasonable.





3.5.1 Practice: fill in the blanks
This is a live exercise: edit the code, click Run Code, and your answer is checked automatically. See Section 1.4.1 if you haven’t used one before.
ph.karno is the physician’s Karnofsky score: 0–100, higher = fitter. Replace each ______, then click Run Code. (The first run downloads the broom package, so it takes a little longer.)


















NoteHint 1





The variable to add is ph.karno. exponentiate needs TRUE to turn coefficients into hazard ratios.











NoteHint 2





cox.zph() takes the fitted model, which here is called m.











TipSolution





m <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ sex + ph.karno, data = lung)
tidy(m, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
exp(10 * coef(m)["ph.karno"])
cox.zph(m)
Women had HR = 0.60 (95% CI 0.43 to 0.84) compared with men with the same Karnofsky score: about a 40% lower hazard. Each 10-point higher score has HR ≈ 0.86, about a 14% lower hazard, so a higher (fitter) score is good news. cox.zph() gives p = 0.005 for ph.karno. Its effect seems to change over follow-up, so a single HR doesn’t tell the whole story. The worked example just below shows what to do about it.

title: 3  Cox proportional hazards regression
section: 3.6 Worked example: an effect that fades
text:
3.6 Worked example: an effect that fades
In the practice above, cox.zph() flagged the Karnofsky score (p = 0.005). Here is how to deal with that, using the second option in the “What to do if PH fails” box: split follow-up time and estimate a separate HR for each period.
First look at the plot. It shows how the log-HR for ph.karno changes over follow-up:

m_karno <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ sex + ph.karno,
                 data = lung)
plot(cox.zph(m_karno)[2], resid = FALSE, lwd = 2)
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)







Figure 3.3: Estimated log-HR for the Karnofsky score over follow-up. The effect is strongest early and fades towards zero.





Beta(t) is the estimated log-HR (per point of the score) at each time. For the first 6 months or so the line is well below zero: a higher score is strongly protective. After that it rises, and reaches zero (no effect) at about a year. So we split each patient’s follow-up at 180 days. survSplit() gives each patient one row per period, with tstart and time marking where each period begins and ends. This is the counting-process form of survival data, which you’ll meet again in Section 4.3:

lung_split <- survSplit(Surv(time, status) ~ ., data = lung,
                        cut = 180, episode = "period")
lung_split$period <- factor(lung_split$period, levels = 1:2,
                            labels = c("0-6 months",
                                       "after 6 months"))

# Patient 1 died at 306 days, so has two rows
lung_split[1:2, c("tstart", "time", "status", "period")]

#>   tstart time status         period
#> 1      0  180      0     0-6 months
#> 2    180  306      1 after 6 months


Then let the effect of ph.karno differ by period. ph.karno:period gives a separate Karnofsky HR for each period:

m_period <- coxph(Surv(tstart, time, status) ~
                    sex + ph.karno:period,
                  data = lung_split)

# HR per 10 points of the Karnofsky score, in each period
exp(10 * coef(m_period)[-1])

#>     ph.karno:period0-6 months ph.karno:periodafter 6 months 
#>                     0.6939382                     0.9612584


In the first 6 months, each 10 points higher on the Karnofsky score goes with a 31% lower hazard (HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.84). After 6 months the effect has almost gone (HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.11). That makes clinical sense: a doctor’s rating of how well a patient is now says a lot about the next few months, and less about the more distant future. A single HR (0.86) would have averaged these two quite different effects. cox.zph(m_period) now shows no evidence against PH (global p = 0.10).
How to choose the cut point? Use the plot, and clinical knowledge, and keep it simple: one or two cut points, chosen before looking at the p-values.

title: 3  Cox proportional hazards regression
text:
3.7 Adjusted survival curves
A Cox model can predict survival curves for chosen covariate patterns. These are often easier to interpret than HRs:

# Two example patients: identical except for sex
newdat <- data.frame(sex = c("Male", "Female"), age = 65, ecog = "1")
pred <- survfit(cox_multi, newdata = newdat)

# One column of predicted survival per patient: put them in a data frame
pred_df <- data.frame(
  time = rep(pred$time, 2),
  surv = c(pred$surv[, 1], pred$surv[, 2]),
  sex  = rep(c("Male", "Female"), each = length(pred$time))
)

ggplot(pred_df, aes(x = time, y = surv, colour = sex)) +
  geom_step(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Male = "#E69F00", Female = "#0072B2")) +
  labs(x = "Days", y = "Predicted survival", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)







Figure 3.4: Model-predicted survival for a 65-year-old with ECOG 1, by sex.





summary() gives the predicted survival at chosen times:

summary(pred, times = 365)

#> Call: survfit(formula = cox_multi, newdata = newdat)
#> 
#>  time n.risk n.event survival1 survival2
#>   365     65     120     0.324     0.522


For a 65-year-old with ECOG 1, the model predicts 1-year survival of 32% for a man (survival1, the first row of newdat) and 52% for a woman (survival2). That’s a 20-percentage-point difference, which is easier to explain than “HR 0.58”. Notice that the gap in survival depends on which patient you pick: for a patient with a worse prognosis, the same HR gives a different gap. These curves are for particular patients, not averages over the whole group.

title: 3  Cox proportional hazards regression
text:
3.8 Writing it up
A sentence template for a hazard ratio:

In a Cox model adjusted for [other variables], [group] was associated with a [X]% [lower/higher] hazard of [event] compared with [reference group] (HR [value], 95% CI [a] to [b], p = [value]).

For a continuous variable, give the HR for a meaningful change, such as 10 years of age. Also say how you checked proportional hazards. Filled in for cox_multi:

In a Cox model adjusted for age and ECOG performance status, women had a 42% lower hazard of death than men (HR 0.58, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.80, p = 0.001). Each additional 10 years of age was associated with a non-significant 12% higher hazard (HR 1.12, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.34). Compared with ECOG 0, the hazard was higher for ECOG 1 (HR 1.51, 95% CI 1.02 to 2.23) and ECOG 2+ (HR 2.50, 95% CI 1.60 to 3.90). Tests and plots of scaled Schoenfeld residuals showed no evidence against proportional hazards.

title: 3  Cox proportional hazards regression
text:
3.9 Good practice

Events per variable. Aim for at least 10–20 events (not patients) per estimated coefficient. A factor with \(k\) levels uses \(k-1\).
Missing data. coxph() silently drops incomplete rows. Check n and number of events in the output. One row was dropped above. Chapter 11 explains when this matters and what to do instead.








NoteGoing further (optional): concordance and ties






Concordance (C-index), shown in summary(). This is the probability that, of two random patients, the model gives the higher risk to the one who dies first. 0.5 = no better than chance, 1 = perfect. Here it is about 0.64.
Ties. When several deaths happen on the same day, the model needs a rule to handle them. R uses the Efron method by default. That’s fine; leave it.

text:
Quick quiz
Choose an answer to each question. You’ll get instant feedback and can change your answer as often as you like.

quiz([
 {
  "q": "A Cox model gives HR = 0.60 for treatment. Which interpretation is correct?",
  "options": [
   "40% fewer treated patients die",
   "Treated patients live 40% longer",
   "At any time, the hazard (instantaneous event rate) in treated patients is 60% of that in controls",
   "60% of treated patients survive"
  ],
  "answer": 2,
  "why": "An HR compares *rates* at each moment. How much that changes the proportion surviving, or survival time, depends on the baseline hazard and the length of follow-up.",
  "hints": [
   "That describes a risk ratio for the proportion who die, which is not the same thing.",
   "An HR isn't a ratio of survival times. (An accelerated failure time model gives those.)",
   "",
   "An HR says nothing directly about the proportion surviving."
  ]
 },
 {
  "q": "The HR for women compared with men is 0.59 (41% lower hazard). What is the HR for men compared with women?",
  "options": [

text:
3.10 Exercise

3.10.1 Exercise 3.1
cox_multi, the model from this chapter (sex + age + ecog), is already fitted in each box. The exercise has three parts. Each box is checked separately.

Part 1: add weight loss
Add wt.loss (weight loss in the last 6 months, in pounds) to the model. Report its HR per 10 lb, and how many observations are used. Then check proportional hazards for the new model (make that the last line).


















NoteHint 1





The formula is the one from cox_multi with + wt.loss added: sex + age + ecog + wt.loss.











NoteHint 2





Proportional hazards are checked with cox.zph(m2).











TipSolution





m2 <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ sex + age + ecog + wt.loss, data = lung)
exp(10 * coef(m2)["wt.loss"])
m2$n
cox.zph(m2)
Adding wt.loss drops patients with missing weight loss, so 213 observations are used instead of 227. Its HR per 10 lb is 0.91 (95% CI 0.80 to 1.04), close to 1 and not significant. cox.zph() shows no evidence against proportional hazards (global p = 0.36).









Part 2: stratify by ECOG
Refit cox_multi stratified by ecog, instead of adjusting for it. How does the HR for sex change?


















NoteHint 1





Stratification uses strata() around the variable’s name.











TipSolution





coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ sex + age + strata(ecog), data = lung)
Stratifying by ECOG gives each ECOG group its own baseline hazard, so there is no HR for ECOG any more. The HR for sex barely changes: 0.57, compared with 0.58 in cox_multi.









Part 3: test for trend
ECOG is ordered (0, 1, 2+). Carry out a test for trend across the ecog groups, and compare it with the omnibus log-rank test (Section 3.4.1 did the same for age bands).


















NoteHint 1





To turn the ordered groups into scores 1, 2, 3, use as.numeric(ecog).











NoteHint 2





The test for trend is the score test, stored as sctest in the model summary.











TipSolution





survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ ecog, data = lung)
trend <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ as.numeric(ecog), data = lung)
summary(trend)$sctest
The omnibus test gives \(\chi^2 \approx 19.0\) on 2 degrees of freedom. The trend test gives \(\chi^2 \approx 17.2\) on just 1 degree of freedom. Almost all of the difference between the groups is a steady worsening of survival as ECOG rises.

title: 3  Cox proportional hazards regression
text:
3.11 Summary






ImportantKey points




The Cox model describes each patient’s hazard as a baseline hazard multiplied by \(\exp(\beta x)\). The baseline hazard’s shape is never specified.
\(\exp(\text{coef})\) is the hazard ratio. The percentage change in hazard is \((\text{HR} - 1) \times 100\%\). Reversing the comparison gives \(1/\text{HR}\).
In a model with several variables, each HR is adjusted for the others. For a factor, each level is compared with the reference level.
A test for trend is the most powerful way to test ordered groups for a steady change in risk.
The model assumes proportional hazards (a constant HR). Check it with cox.zph() and its plots. If it fails, stratify, split follow-up time, or use another effect measure.



Answering the question. After adjusting for age and ECOG, women had a hazard ratio of 0.58 (95% CI 0.41 to 0.80) compared with men. At any point in time, their hazard of death was about 42% lower. The difference wasn’t explained by age or fitness.

text:
4.2 Trap 2: competing risks
Suppose the event you care about is relapse of a cancer, but some patients die before they relapse. What do you do with those deaths?
The tempting answer is to treat them as censored: they didn’t relapse during follow-up, after all. But a patient who has died can never relapse. Censoring them tells KM to assume they’re still at risk of relapse, just unobserved, like someone who moved away. These events are called competing risks, because the two events compete: whichever happens first prevents the other.
The result is that 1 − KM overestimates the probability of the event. This simulation has relapse and death without relapse equally common:

set.seed(2026)
n <- 1000
relapse_time <- rexp(n, rate = 0.15)    # years
death_time   <- rexp(n, rate = 0.15)    # death without relapse
end_time     <- runif(n, 2, 6)          # end of follow-up

cr <- data.frame(time = pmin(relapse_time, death_time, end_time))
cr$event <- ifelse(cr$time == relapse_time, "relapse",
            ifelse(cr$time == death_time, "death", "censored"))
cr$event <- factor(cr$event, levels = c("censored", "relapse", "death"))

table(cr$event)

#> 
#> censored  relapse    death 
#>      323      340      337


First the wrong way. Treat each kind of event in turn as the outcome, censoring the other, and look at 1 − KM at 5 years:

km_relapse <- survfit(Surv(time, event == "relapse") ~ 1, data = cr)
km_death   <- survfit(Surv(time, event == "death") ~ 1, data = cr)

1 - summary(km_relapse, times = 5)$surv     # "risk" of relapse

#> [1] 0.520549

1 - summary(km_death, times = 5)$surv       # "risk" of death

#> [1] 0.5218315


That says 52% relapse by 5 years and 52% die without relapsing: 104% of patients. That’s impossible, because no patient can do both.
The right way is the cumulative incidence function (CIF): the probability of having had each kind of event by a given time, allowing for the fact that the other event can happen first. survfit() calculates it when the event variable is a factor whose first level is censoring:

cif <- survfit(Surv(time, event) ~ 1, data = cr)
summary(cif, times = 5)

#> Call: survfit(formula = Surv(time, event) ~ 1, data = cr)
#> 
#>  time n.risk n.event Pr((s0)) Pr(relapse) Pr(death)
#>     5     48     669    0.229       0.386     0.385








NoteHow to read this output




Pr((s0)) is the probability of having had neither event yet (here 23%). (s0) stands for the starting state.
Pr(relapse) and Pr(death) are the cumulative incidences: 39% and 38% at 5 years.
The three add up to 100%, as they should.




plot_data <- rbind(
  data.frame(time   = km_relapse$time,
             risk   = 1 - km_relapse$surv,
             method = "1 - KM (deaths censored)"),
  data.frame(time   = cif$time,
             risk   = cif$pstate[, "relapse"],
             method = "Cumulative incidence")
)

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = time, y = risk, colour = method)) +
  geom_step(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#D55E00", "#0072B2")) +
  labs(x = "Years", y = "Probability of relapse", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")







Figure 4.1: 1 − KM overstates the probability of relapse when some patients die first.





The gap grows over time, as more patients are removed by the competing event. It matters most when the competing event is common, for example in older patients, or for cause-specific outcomes such as death from cancer (where death from other causes competes).
What does 1 − KM actually estimate? The probability of relapse in a hypothetical world where nobody could die first, and even that only under strong assumptions. That’s occasionally the question you want, but usually it isn’t.

4.2.1 Interactive app: when does it matter?
How badly 1 − KM overstates the risk depends on how common the competing event is, and on how long patients are followed. In this app you set the rate of the event of interest (say relapse) and of the competing event (say death), both per year. The solid lines are estimated from one simulated study. The dashed lines are the truth:

blue dashed: the true probability of relapse, which the cumulative incidence (solid blue) should follow;
orange dashed: the probability of relapse in a world where nobody could die first, which is what 1 − KM (solid orange) actually estimates.


import {simCompeting, competingCurves, stepAt, simImmortal, immortalEstimates} from "./js/extras.js"








viewof crScen = Inputs.radio(["Default", "No competing event", "Common competing event", "Rare event, common competing event", "Short follow-up"], {value: "Default", label: "Scenario"})
crP = ({"Default": {}, "No competing event": {"rate2": 0}, "Common competing event": {"rate2": 0.4}, "Rare event, common competing event": {"rate1": 0.02, "rate2": 0.12, "fu": 20, "at": 15}, "Short follow-up": {"fu": 2, "at": 1.5}})[crScen]
viewof cr = Inputs.form({
  rate1: Inputs.range([0.01, 0.5], {value: crP.rate1 ?? 0.15, step: 0.01, label: "Rate of the event of interest (per year)"}),
  rate2: Inputs.range([0, 0.5], {value: crP.rate2 ?? 0.15, step: 0.01, label: "Rate of the competing event (per year)"}),
  fu:    Inputs.range([1, 20], {value: crP.fu ?? 6, step: 1, label: "Maximum follow-up (years)"}),
  at:    Inputs.range([0.5, 20], {value: crP.at ?? 5, step: 0.5, label: "Read off the risk at (years)"}),
  n:     Inputs.range([200, 3000], {value: crP.n ?? 1000, step: 100, label: "Patients"}),
  seed:  Inputs.range([1, 100], {value: crP.seed ?? 1, step: 1, label: "Random seed (new study)"})
}, {template: formGrid})























crRows = competingCurves(simCompeting({n: cr.n, rate1: cr.rate1, rate2: cr.rate2, fu: cr.fu, seed: cr.seed}))
crTruth = {
  const pts = [], tot = cr.rate1 + cr.rate2;
  for (let t = 0; t <= cr.fu; t += cr.fu / 200) {
    pts.push({time: t, value: cr.rate1 / tot * (1 - Math.exp(-tot * t)), line: "True risk (with competing event)"});
    pts.push({time: t, value: 1 - Math.exp(-cr.rate1 * t), line: "Risk if nobody could die first"});
  }
  return pts;
}
crAt = Math.min(cr.at, cr.fu)























Plot.plot({
  height: 330, y: {domain: [0, 1], grid: true, label: "Probability of the event of interest"},
  x: {label: "Years →", domain: [0, cr.fu]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["1 − KM (competing events censored)", "Cumulative incidence"], range: ["#D55E00", "#0072B2"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(crTruth.filter(d => d.line === "True risk (with competing event)"), {x: "time", y: "value", stroke: "#0072B2", strokeDasharray: "5,4", strokeWidth: 1.5}),
    Plot.line(crTruth.filter(d => d.line === "Risk if nobody could die first"), {x: "time", y: "value", stroke: "#D55E00", strokeDasharray: "5,4", strokeWidth: 1.5}),
    Plot.line(crRows, {x: "time", y: "oneMinusKM", stroke: () => "1 − KM (competing events censored)", strokeWidth: 2.2, curve: "step-after"}),
    Plot.line(crRows, {x: "time", y: "cif", stroke: () => "Cumulative incidence", strokeWidth: 2.2, curve: "step-after"}),
    Plot.ruleX([crAt], {stroke: "#888", strokeDasharray: "2,3"})
  ]
})







{
  const km = stepAt(crRows, "oneMinusKM", crAt), ci = stepAt(crRows, "cif", crAt);
  const tot = cr.rate1 + cr.rate2;
  const truth = cr.rate1 / tot * (1 - Math.exp(-tot * crAt));
  const pct = v => (100 * v).toFixed(1) + "%";
  return html`<div class="estimates">
  <div class="est"><span>True risk at ${crAt} years</span><b>${pct(truth)}</b><small> </small></div>
  <div class="est bad"><span>1 − KM</span><b>${pct(km)}</b><small>${ci > 0 ? (km / ci).toFixed(2) + " × the cumulative incidence" : ""}</small></div>
  <div class="est good"><span>Cumulative incidence</span><b>${pct(ci)}</b><small> </small></div>
  </div>`;
}













TipThings to try



For each one, predict first, then pick the scenario and check.

Predict: if nobody can die first, will the two estimates differ? Then pick No competing event.
Predict: what happens to the gap when the competing event becomes more common? Then pick Common competing event.
Predict: with a rare event of interest, a common competing event and long follow-up (like the MGUS example below), how far off is 1 − KM? Then pick Rare event, common competing event.
Predict: does the problem matter much in a short study? Then pick Short follow-up.









NoteAnswers: what you should see






No. With no competing event, the two curves are identical (both 52% at 5 years, truth 53%). Competing risks only matter when there’s something to compete with.
The gap grows. With a competing event rate of 0.4 per year, 1 − KM says 52% at 5 years, but the true risk is only 26%: 1 − KM is about double the cumulative incidence (26%). Notice that 1 − KM hardly changes from the default. It estimates the risk in a world without the competing event, so the competing event doesn’t affect it, which is exactly the problem.
About double. At 15 years, 1 − KM says 25%, but the true risk is about 13% (cumulative incidence 13%). Over long follow-up, most patients have the competing event first.
Not much. At 1.5 years, 1 − KM gives 20% and the cumulative incidence 18% (truth 18%). Few patients have had time to die first. The gap grows with follow-up.






4.2.2 Real data: progression of MGUS
The mgus2 dataset, in the survival package, follows 1384 people with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS), a blood condition that can progress to a cancer of plasma cells. Most of these patients are elderly, so many die of other causes before MGUS has the chance to progress. The data have two time columns:

ptime and pstat: time to progression (in months), and whether it happened (1) or not (0);
futime and death: time to death or last follow-up, and whether the patient died.

First we combine them into one time and one event, with three possible values:

mg <- survival::mgus2

# Time to the first event: progression if it happened, otherwise death or last follow-up
mg$etime <- ifelse(mg$pstat == 1, mg$ptime, mg$futime)

# Which event came first
mg$event <- ifelse(mg$pstat == 1, "progression",
            ifelse(mg$death == 1, "death", "censored"))
mg$event <- factor(mg$event, levels = c("censored", "progression", "death"))

table(mg$event)

#> 
#>    censored progression       death 
#>         409         115         860


Only 115 patients progressed, but 860 died first. Compare the two estimates of the risk of progression at 10, 20 and 30 years (120, 240 and 360 months):

# Wrong: deaths treated as censored
km_prog <- survfit(Surv(etime, event == "progression") ~ 1, data = mg)
1 - summary(km_prog, times = c(120, 240, 360))$surv

#> [1] 0.09522166 0.20956162 0.42483694

# Right: cumulative incidence
cif_mg <- survfit(Surv(etime, event) ~ 1, data = mg)
summary(cif_mg, times = c(120, 240, 360))

#> Call: survfit(formula = Surv(etime, event) ~ 1, data = mg)
#> 
#>  time n.risk n.event Pr((s0)) Pr(progression) Pr(death)
#>   120    424     781   0.4045          0.0637     0.532
#>   240     57     177   0.1762          0.0998     0.724
#>   360      3      15   0.0818          0.1340     0.784


1 − KM says that 42% of patients will have progressed by 30 years. The cumulative incidence is 13%. The difference is the patients who died first: 1 − KM pretends they were still at risk of progression for decades. For a patient being told about their risk, the second number is the relevant one.


4.2.3 Comparing groups: rates or probabilities?
With competing risks there are two different questions you can ask about a group difference, and two kinds of Cox model to answer them:

A cause-specific Cox model treats competing events as censored. That sounds like the mistake above, but for hazard ratios it’s fine. It answers: “among patients still alive and event-free, does the group change the rate of progression?” This is usually the question when you want to know whether something causes the event, or whether a treatment works.
A Fine–Gray model compares the cumulative incidence itself. It answers: “does the group change the probability of progression, in a world where patients can also die?” This is usually the question for prediction and planning.

The two can give different answers. Here’s the cause-specific model for progression, and for death, comparing men with women and adjusting for age:

# Cause-specific Cox model for progression (deaths censored)
coxph(Surv(etime, event == "progression") ~ sex + age,
      data = mg) |>
  broom::tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value)

#> # A tibble: 2 x 5
#>   term  estimate conf.low conf.high p.value
#>   <chr>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 sexM     0.975    0.674      1.41   0.894
#> 2 age      1.01     0.997      1.03   0.114

# Cause-specific Cox model for death (progressions censored)
coxph(Surv(etime, event == "death") ~ sex + age,
      data = mg) |>
  broom::tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value)

#> # A tibble: 2 x 5
#>   term  estimate conf.low conf.high  p.value
#>   <chr>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 sexM      1.48     1.29      1.70 1.68e- 8
#> 2 age       1.07     1.06      1.07 1.06e-71


Among patients still alive and progression-free, men and women progress at the same rate (HR for men 0.98, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.41). But men die faster (HR 1.48). So fewer men live long enough to progress, and the probability of progression is lower in men: by 10 years, 5.5% of men have progressed, compared with 7.4% of women. Both statements are true. They answer different questions.







NoteGoing further (optional): a Fine–Gray model in R





finegray() reshapes the data, and coxph() with the weights it creates fits the Fine–Gray model:

fg <- finegray(Surv(etime, event) ~ sex + age, data = mg,
               etype = "progression")
coxph(Surv(fgstart, fgstop, fgstatus) ~ sex + age,
      weights = fgwt, data = fg) |>
  broom::tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value)

#> # A tibble: 2 x 5
#>   term  estimate conf.low conf.high p.value
#>   <chr>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 sexM     0.771    0.540     1.10  0.153  
#> 2 age      0.983    0.972     0.994 0.00175


The HR for men is now 0.77 (95% CI 0.54 to 1.10). This subdistribution hazard ratio reflects the lower probability of progression in men, which comes partly from their higher death rate. It is harder to interpret than a cause-specific HR, which is why both are often reported. See Austin et al. (2016) and the survival package’s vignette (Therneau et al., n.d.-a).






4.2.4 Practice: cumulative incidence by sex
This is a live exercise: edit the code, click Run Code, and your answer is checked automatically. See Section 1.4.1 if you haven’t used one before.
The mgus2 data are loaded as mg. Build the time and event variables, then estimate the cumulative incidence of progression and death by sex, and look at them at 10 years (120 months). Replace each ______, then click Run Code.


















NoteHint 1





The first level of the factor must be censoring: "censored".











NoteHint 2





Surv(etime, event), with the factor as the event, gives cumulative incidences. 10 years is 120 months.











TipSolution





mg$etime <- ifelse(mg$pstat == 1, mg$ptime, mg$futime)
mg$event <- ifelse(mg$pstat == 1, "progression",
            ifelse(mg$death == 1, "death", "censored"))
mg$event <- factor(mg$event, levels = c("censored", "progression", "death"))
cif_sex <- survfit(Surv(etime, event) ~ sex, data = mg)
summary(cif_sex, times = 120)
By 10 years, 7.4% of women and 5.5% of men had progressed, while 48% of women and 58% of men had died without progressing. Men are less likely to progress mainly because more of them die first: the cause-specific model showed no difference in the rate of progression.
