title: 4  Common traps: censoring, competing events and time zero
text:
4.3 Trap 3: immortal time bias
Kaplan–Meier curves compare groups that are defined at time zero: sex, age group, the treatment someone was randomised to. A tempting mistake is to group patients by something that only happens later, such as “received a transplant”, “responded to treatment” or “ever took drug X”. This gives the “yes” group a large, entirely artificial survival advantage.

4.3.1 Why is it called “immortal” time?
Picture the timelines of two patients who would both start treatment a few months after diagnosis:
           time zero      treatment starts
              |                |
Patient A:    |--- waiting ----|==== treated ====| died
Patient B:    |-- waiting --X  (died before treatment)
Patient A ends up in the “treated” group. But to get there, A had to survive the whole waiting period. Nobody in the treated group can have died while waiting: anyone who did, like patient B, never started treatment and ends up in the “untreated” group instead.
So the waiting time of every treated patient is time during which they could not die, as if they were temporarily immortal. Hence the name. The naive analysis makes two errors at once:

it counts that immortal time as treated follow-up, so the treated group gets credit for survival that has nothing to do with the treatment;
the deaths that happened during waiting periods, like patient B’s, are all counted in the untreated group, which makes it look worse.

Both errors push in the same direction: the treatment looks protective even if it does nothing at all.


4.3.2 A treatment that does nothing
This simulation makes 1000 patients whose survival has nothing to do with treatment. Each patient would start treatment at a random time in the first 2 years, but only if they’re still alive by then.

set.seed(42)
n <- 1000

# Survival times, unrelated to treatment
death_time <- rexp(n, rate = 0.35)

# When each patient's treatment would start
start_time <- runif(n, 0, 2)

# Follow-up ends at 3 years
imm <- data.frame(
  time   = pmin(death_time, 3),
  status = as.numeric(death_time <= 3)
)

# "Ever treated" only if still alive when treatment was due
treated_in_time <- start_time < imm$time
imm$ever_treated <- factor(treated_in_time,
                           levels = c(FALSE, TRUE),
                           labels = c("Never", "Ever"))

survfit2(Surv(time, status) ~ ever_treated, data = imm) |>
  ggsurvfit(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#D55E00", "#0072B2")) +
  labs(x = "Years since time zero")







Figure 4.2: Grouping by ‘ever treated’ makes a useless treatment look dramatically protective.





The curves could hardly be further apart, and the log-rank test gives a tiny p-value. Yet the treatment does nothing. Notice too that every “untreated” patient died: the only way to stay untreated was to die before your treatment was due to start.
This is not just a textbook curiosity. A well-known 2001 study reported that Oscar-winning actors lived almost 4 years longer than other actors, but it counted winners’ lives from birth, including the years before they won. Nobody can die before winning an Oscar and still be a winner. A reanalysis that handled the immortal time properly found a difference of about 1 year, with a confidence interval that included zero (Sylvestre et al. 2006).


4.3.3 How to avoid it
There are two standard fixes. Both make sure that patients are only counted as “treated” from the moment they actually start treatment.
A landmark analysis. Pick a time point (the landmark), e.g. 1 year. Keep only patients still alive and followed at the landmark, classify them by their status at that time, and start the clock again there:

# Landmark at 1 year: keep patients still alive at 1 year,
# grouped by whether they had started treatment by then
imm$start_time <- start_time
lm1 <- subset(imm, time > 1)
lm1$treated_by_1 <- as.numeric(lm1$start_time < 1)

survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ treated_by_1, data = lm1)

#> Call:
#> survdiff(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ treated_by_1, data = lm1)
#> 
#>                  N Observed Expected (O-E)^2/E (O-E)^2/V
#> treated_by_1=0 393      193      186     0.297     0.616
#> treated_by_1=1 343      166      173     0.318     0.616
#> 
#>  Chisq= 0.6  on 1 degrees of freedom, p= 0.4


At the landmark, the two groups have the same survival (p = 0.4), which is the correct answer. The drawbacks are that the result depends on the landmark you choose, and patients who start treatment after it are counted as untreated.
A time-varying covariate in a Cox model. Each patient counts as untreated until the day they start treatment, and treated afterwards. To do this, each patient’s follow-up is split into periods, one row per period. A patient who starts treatment at 0.2 years and dies at 1.9 years gets two rows: untreated from 0 to 0.2, and treated from 0.2 to 1.9. The tmerge() function in the survival package builds these rows:

imm$id <- seq_len(nrow(imm))

# Treatment start time, or NA if the patient never started
imm$treat_start <- ifelse(imm$start_time < imm$time, imm$start_time, NA)

tv <- tmerge(imm[, c("id", "time", "status")], imm, id = id,
             death   = event(time, status),
             treated = tdc(treat_start))

head(tv[, c("id", "tstart", "tstop", "death", "treated")])

#>   id    tstart     tstop death treated
#> 1  1 0.0000000 0.5666766     1       0
#> 2  2 0.0000000 0.2195664     0       0
#> 3  2 0.2195664 1.8882721     1       1
#> 4  3 0.0000000 0.7392050     0       0
#> 5  3 0.7392050 0.8099744     1       1
#> 6  4 0.0000000 0.1091197     1       0








TipHow to read this output




Each row is one period of a patient’s follow-up, from tstart to tstop.
treated is 0 before treatment starts and 1 afterwards. tdc() stands for time-dependent covariate.
death is 1 only in the period that ends with a death.
Patient 2 started treatment at 0.22 years and died at 1.89 years, so has two rows. Patient 1 died at 0.57 years, before their treatment was due, so has one row and is never treated.



The Cox model then uses the counting-process form of Surv(), with a start and a stop time:

coxph(Surv(tstart, tstop, death) ~ treated, data = tv) |>
  broom::tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value)

#> # A tibble: 1 x 5
#>   term    estimate conf.low conf.high p.value
#>   <chr>      <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 treated    0.947    0.759      1.18   0.632


The HR is 0.95 (95% CI 0.76 to 1.18): close to 1, the truth. The waiting time is now correctly counted as untreated time.


4.3.4 Interactive app: watching immortal time happen
Here you can see the immortal time, and how much it distorts the naive analysis. Some patients would be offered treatment at some point during their first few years of follow-up; the rest never would. Each line in the timeline is a patient:

an orange stretch is waiting time before treatment starts: immortal time, since a patient who died then would never have joined the treated group;
a blue stretch is time on treatment;
a grey line is a patient who was never treated. A small orange tick past the end of a grey line marks where an untreated patient would have started treatment if they hadn’t died first, like patient B above.

The estimates compare the naive analysis (grouping by “ever treated”) with a landmark analysis and a time-varying Cox model.


viewof imScen = Inputs.radio(["Treatment does nothing", "Short wait (up to 3 months)", "Long wait (up to 3 years)", "Treatment really works (HR 0.7)", "Treatment is harmful (HR 1.5)", "Everyone is eventually treated"], {value: "Treatment does nothing", label: "Scenario"})
imP = ({"Treatment does nothing": {}, "Short wait (up to 3 months)": {"wait": 0.25}, "Long wait (up to 3 years)": {"wait": 3}, "Treatment really works (HR 0.7)": {"hr": 0.7}, "Treatment is harmful (HR 1.5)": {"hr": 1.5}, "Everyone is eventually treated": {"p": 1}})[imScen]
viewof im = Inputs.form({
  hr:   Inputs.range([0.5, 2], {value: imP.hr ?? 1, step: 0.05, label: "TRUE hazard ratio for treatment"}),
  wait: Inputs.range([0.25, 3], {value: imP.wait ?? 2, step: 0.25, label: "Treatment starts within (years)"}),
  p:    Inputs.range([0.2, 1], {value: imP.p ?? 0.5, step: 0.1, label: "Proportion who would ever start"}),
  L:    Inputs.range([0.25, 2], {value: imP.L ?? 1, step: 0.25, label: "Landmark (years)"}),
  n:    Inputs.range([200, 1000], {value: imP.n ?? 400, step: 100, label: "Patients"}),
  seed: Inputs.range([1, 100], {value: imP.seed ?? 4, step: 1, label: "Random seed (new study)"})
}, {template: formGrid})























imData = simImmortal({n: im.n, rate: 0.35, hr: im.hr, maxWait: im.wait, fu: 3, seed: im.seed, pTreat: im.p})
imEst = immortalEstimates(imData, im.L)
















{
  const show = imData.slice(0, 30);
  const segs = [];
  for (const p of show) {
    if (p.treated) {
      segs.push({id: p.id, x1: 0, x2: p.start, kind: "Waiting (immortal) time"});
      segs.push({id: p.id, x1: p.start, x2: p.time, kind: "On treatment"});
    } else segs.push({id: p.id, x1: 0, x2: p.time, kind: "Never treated"});
  }
  const ticks = show.filter(p => !p.treated && p.start < 3);
  return Plot.plot({
    height: 120 + 13 * show.length, marginLeft: 50,
    x: {label: "Years since time zero →", domain: [0, 3]},
    y: {label: "Patient", domain: show.map(p => p.id), tickFormat: d => d},
    color: {legend: true, domain: ["Waiting (immortal) time", "On treatment", "Never treated"], range: ["#E69F00", "#0072B2", "#999999"]},
    marks: [
      Plot.ruleY(segs, {y: "id", x1: "x1", x2: "x2", stroke: "kind", strokeWidth: 3}),
      Plot.dot(show.filter(p => p.status), {y: "id", x: "time", fill: "black", r: 3.5}),
      Plot.dot(show.filter(p => !p.status), {y: "id", x: "time", stroke: "black", symbol: "times", r: 4}),
      Plot.tickX(ticks, {y: "id", x: "start", stroke: "#E69F00", strokeWidth: 2})
    ]
  });
}

  const f = e => isFinite(e.hr) ? e.hr.toFixed(2) : "–";
  const ci = e => isFinite(e.hr) ? `95% CI ${e.lower.toFixed(2)} to ${e.upper.toFixed(2)}` : "";
  const nT = imData.filter(p => p.treated).length;
  const unt = imData.filter(p => !p.treated);
  const diedWaiting = unt.filter(p => p.start < Infinity).length;
  return html`<div class="estimates">
  <div class="est"><span>True HR</span><b>${im.hr.toFixed(2)}</b><small> </small></div>
  <div class="est bad"><span>Naive: ever vs never treated</span><b>${f(imEst.naive)}</b><small>${ci(imEst.naive)}</small></div>
  <div class="est good"><span>Landmark at ${im.L} year${im.L === 1 ? "" : "s"}</span><b>${f(imEst.lm)}</b><small>${isFinite(imEst.lm.hr) ? ci(imEst.lm) : "Everyone alive at the landmark is in the same group: choose an earlier landmark"}</small></div>
  <div class="est good"><span>Time-varying Cox model</span><b>${f(imEst.tv)}</b><small>${ci(imEst.tv)}</small></div>
  </div>
  <p style="margin-top:.5em">${nT} patients started treatment and ${unt.length} never did.
  <span style="color:#D55E00">${diedWaiting} of the never-treated patients died while waiting for treatment that was due to start.</span>
  The landmark analysis uses the ${imEst.nL} patients still alive at ${im.L} year${im.L === 1 ? "" : "s"}.</p>`;
}













TipThings to try



For each one, predict first, then pick the scenario and check.

Predict: if treatment does nothing, what will the naive HR be? Then look at the default scenario, Treatment does nothing, and find some orange ticks past the end of grey lines.
Predict: does the bias get bigger or smaller if treatment starts sooner? Or later? Then pick Short wait (up to 3 months) and Long wait (up to 3 years).
Predict: if treatment is genuinely harmful (HR 1.5), could the naive analysis still make it look protective? Then pick Treatment is harmful (HR 1.5). Try Treatment really works (HR 0.7) too.
Predict: what happens if everyone would eventually be treated, as in the simulation earlier in this section? Then pick Everyone is eventually treated.
On the default scenario, move the landmark between 0.5 and 1.5 years. What happens to the landmark estimate and to the number of patients it uses?









NoteAnswers: what you should see






About 0.43, a 57% lower hazard, from a treatment that does nothing (95% CI 0.32 to 0.57). 54 of the 274 never-treated patients died while waiting for treatment: each of those deaths is counted against the “never treated” group. The landmark analysis (1.03) and the time-varying model (0.99) both get it right.
The longer the wait, the bigger the bias. With treatment starting within 3 months, there’s little immortal time and the naive HR is 0.78. With waits of up to 3 years, it’s 0.35. The corrected methods stay close to 1 (allowing for chance).
Yes. With a true HR of 1.5, the naive HR is 0.58: a harmful treatment looks protective. The time-varying model gets 1.45, close to the truth. With a true HR of 0.7, the naive analysis exaggerates the benefit (0.29), while the time-varying model gives 0.64. The landmark estimate (0.86) is pulled towards 1: some patients in its “untreated” group start treatment after the landmark and benefit from it.
The bias becomes extreme: naive HR 0.07. Now the only way to be “never treated” is to die before treatment is due, which is what the simulation earlier in this section showed. The time-varying model still gets 0.96.
An earlier landmark uses more patients (324 at 0.5 years) but leaves more patients to start treatment after it. A later landmark uses fewer (225 at 1.5 years), so the estimate is less precise. Here all of them are close to the truth of 1 (1.05, 1.03 and 1.16). The time-varying model avoids having to choose.






4.3.5 Real data: the Stanford heart transplant study
The classic example comes from the Stanford heart transplant programme, which started in 1967. Patients were accepted onto the programme and then waited for a donor heart. Some received one; others died while waiting. Early analyses compared patients who received a transplant with those who didn’t, and found a huge benefit. Later analyses showed that much of that benefit was immortal time (Gail 1972; Crowley and Hu 1977).
The survival package has the data in two forms. jasa has one row per patient. Here’s the naive analysis, comparing patients who ever had a transplant with those who didn’t, from the day they joined the programme:

jasa <- survival::jasa
jasa$futime <- as.numeric(jasa$fu.date - jasa$accept.dt)   # days in the programme

coxph(Surv(futime, fustat) ~ transplant, data = jasa) |>
  broom::tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value)

#> # A tibble: 1 x 5
#>   term       estimate conf.low conf.high      p.value
#>   <chr>         <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>        <dbl>
#> 1 transplant    0.266    0.165     0.429 0.0000000569


A hazard ratio of 0.27: transplant appears to cut the hazard of death by nearly three-quarters. But the patients who died while waiting all count in the “no transplant” group. heart has the same patients in counting-process form, already split at the time of transplant, so transplant is a time-varying covariate. You’ll fit that model in the exercise at the end of this chapter.
The key lesson for all of this: make sure time zero is the same moment for everyone, and that group membership is known at that moment (Chapter 1). In the simulated cohort in Chapters 5–7, everyone’s clock starts when the treatment decision is made, so there is no immortal time.

text:
4.4 Exercise

4.4.1 Exercise 4.1
The Stanford heart transplant data are loaded in two forms: jasa, with one row per patient, and heart, with each patient’s follow-up split at the time of their transplant. The exercise has two parts, each checked separately.

Part 1: the naive analysis
Fit a Cox model comparing patients who ever had a transplant (transplant) with those who didn’t, using futime (days in the programme) and fustat (1 = died). Make the model the last line.


















NoteHint 1





The time is futime and the event is fustat.











TipSolution





coxph(Surv(futime, fustat) ~ transplant, data = jasa)
The naive HR is 0.27 (95% CI 0.17 to 0.43): transplant looks as if it cuts the hazard of death by 73%. But every patient who died while waiting for a heart counts in the “no transplant” group.









Part 2: transplant as a time-varying covariate
In heart, each row is a period of follow-up from start to stop (days), event is 1 if the period ended in death, and transplant is 0 before the transplant and 1 afterwards. Look at the first few rows, then fit the Cox model with transplant as a time-varying covariate (make that the last line). How does the HR compare with part 1?


















NoteHint 1





The counting-process form of Surv() takes three arguments: the start time, the stop time and the event.











NoteHint 2





Surv(start, stop, event).











TipSolution





head(heart)
coxph(Surv(start, stop, event) ~ transplant, data = heart)
Patients who received a transplant have two rows: one before the transplant (transplant = 0) and one after (transplant = 1). With transplant as a time-varying covariate, the HR is 1.14 (95% CI 0.63 to 2.05). There is no clear evidence that transplant improved survival in these data. The apparent 73% reduction was almost entirely immortal time bias.
(This doesn’t show that heart transplantation is useless: results have improved enormously since the 1960s, and it is now a standard treatment. The point is that the naive comparison is badly biased.)

text:
4.5 Summary






ImportantKey points




Informative censoring: if the patients who drop out differ in risk from those who stay, KM and Cox estimates are biased. It can’t be detected from the survival data alone, so compare the patients who were lost with those who stayed, and allow for measured reasons for drop-out.
Competing risks: treating a competing event (such as death) as censoring makes 1 − KM overstate the risk. Use the cumulative incidence function, from survfit() with a factor event. A cause-specific Cox model compares rates; a Fine–Gray model compares probabilities.
Immortal time bias: grouping patients by something that happens after time zero gives that group a spurious advantage. Use a landmark analysis or a time-varying covariate (tmerge() and Surv(start, stop, event)).
In every case, think carefully about who is at risk, and when, and make time zero the same for everyone.



Answering the question. All three traps produce clean-looking output and convincing p-values. In the examples here, informative censoring made 2-year survival look like 50% when it was 35%; ignoring competing deaths tripled the apparent 30-year risk of MGUS progression, from 13% to 42%; and immortal time turned a heart transplant HR of 1.14 (Exercise 4.1) into an apparent 73% reduction in the hazard of death. The fixes are standard and use the same survival package, as long as you recognise the trap first.

title: 5  Confounding and propensity scores
text:
5.1 The problem: confounding
In a randomised trial, chance alone decides who gets treated. So treated and untreated patients are similar on average in every way, measured or not, and any difference in outcomes can be put down to the treatment.
In observational data, treatment decisions depend on patient characteristics. Sicker patients may be more likely to get a new drug (confounding by indication), or less likely to get surgery. A confounder is a variable that affects both treatment and outcome. If we ignore confounders, a treatment that helps can look harmful.

title: 5  Confounding and propensity scores
section: 5.2 Meet the data: a simulated observational cohort
text:
5.2 Meet the data: a simulated observational cohort
To learn these methods, we need data where we know the right answer. Then we can check whether each method recovers it. Real observational data can’t do that, so for the rest of the book we use a simulated cohort. It’s made by the function simulate_cohort(), which is in the file simulate_cohort.R. If you haven’t already, download it into your project folder (see Section 3).
The scenario. 2,000 patients are seen in routine care. Some are started on a new preventive treatment and some aren’t. The decision isn’t random: clinicians are more likely to treat patients who seem at higher risk. All patients are then followed for up to 8 years, until death or censoring.



Variable
Description




id
Patient identifier


age
Age at baseline (years)


female
1 = female, 0 = male


diabetes
1 = has diabetes (more common at older ages)


bmi
Body mass index (kg/m²)


smoker
1 = current smoker


treated
1 = received the treatment, 0 = did not


time
Follow-up time (years)


status
1 = died, 0 = censored



How the data were generated. There are two steps, and each one uses the same baseline variables:

Who gets treated. The probability of treatment rises with age, diabetes, BMI and smoking, and is a little lower for women. This is confounding by indication.
Who dies, and when. Survival times follow a proportional hazards model. Age, diabetes, BMI and smoking also raise the hazard of death, and women have a lower hazard. Treatment reduces the hazard of death by 30%: the true conditional hazard ratio is 0.70. (Conditional means comparing patients who have the same values of the other variables. Chapter 7 explains why that detail matters.)

Censoring comes from staggered entry (follow-up ends 3–8 years after a patient joins) plus random loss to follow-up. It is unrelated to prognosis, so it is non-informative.
So every baseline variable is a confounder: it pushes patients towards treatment and towards death. The treatment truly works, but the treated patients start out sicker.


Show the simulation code
# simulate_cohort.R ----------------------------------------------------------
#
# Simulates an *observational* cohort in which patients choose (or are given)
# a treatment non-randomly, and are then followed up until death or censoring.
#
# Because we simulate the data ourselves we KNOW the truth, so we can check
# whether each method recovers it. This is the best way to learn these tools.
#
#   * Older patients, diabetics, people with higher BMI and smokers are MORE
#     likely to be treated  -> confounding by indication.
#   * The same factors also raise the hazard of death.
#   * The true conditional hazard ratio for treatment is 0.70 (a 30% lower
#     hazard of death, holding the covariates fixed).
#
# Time is measured in years.

simulate_cohort <- function(n = 2000, hr_treat = 0.70, seed = 2026) {
  set.seed(seed)

  age      <- round(pmin(pmax(rnorm(n, 65, 10), 35), 95))
  female   <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.45)
  diabetes <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-1.4 + 0.04 * (age - 65)))
  bmi      <- round(rnorm(n, 28, 4.5), 1)
  smoker   <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.25)

  # --- Treatment assignment (the "propensity score" model) ------------------
  lp_treat <- -0.6 + 0.06 * (age - 65) + 1.0 * diabetes + 0.08 * (bmi - 28) -
    0.3 * female + 0.4 * smoker
  treated <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(lp_treat))

  # --- Survival time: Weibull proportional hazards --------------------------
  lp_death <- log(hr_treat) * treated + 0.06 * (age - 65) + 0.6 * diabetes +
    0.03 * (bmi - 28) - 0.25 * female + 0.55 * smoker
  shape  <- 1.2
  lambda <- 0.05                       # baseline hazard scale (per year)
  t_event <- (-log(runif(n)) / (lambda * exp(lp_death)))^(1 / shape)

  # --- Censoring: staggered entry (administrative) + random loss to follow-up
  t_admin   <- runif(n, 3, 8)          # study ends 3-8 years after entry
  t_dropout <- rexp(n, rate = 0.04)
  t_cens    <- pmin(t_admin, t_dropout)

  time   <- pmin(t_event, t_cens)
  status <- as.integer(t_event <= t_cens)

  data.frame(
    id       = seq_len(n),
    age, female, diabetes, bmi, smoker,
    treated,
    time     = round(time, 3),
    status
  )
}


Load the function, then create the cohort and look at it:

source("simulate_cohort.R")    # run this first: it loads simulate_cohort()


cohort <- simulate_cohort(n = 2000, seed = 2026)
head(cohort)

#>   id age female diabetes  bmi smoker treated  time status
#> 1  1  70      1        0 33.6      0       0 5.542      1
#> 2  2  54      0        0 26.5      0       0 3.243      0
#> 3  3  66      1        0 36.4      0       0 5.553      0
#> 4  4  64      0        0 20.8      0       0 6.189      1
#> 5  5  58      0        1 24.5      1       0 1.482      1
#> 6  6  40      0        0 30.3      0       0 5.723      0

# Patients, deaths, and baseline characteristics by treatment group
cohort |>
  group_by(treated) |>
  summarise(n = n(), deaths = sum(status),
            age = mean(age), female = mean(female), diabetes = mean(diabetes),
            bmi = mean(bmi), smoker = mean(smoker))

#> # A tibble: 2 x 8
#>   treated     n deaths   age female diabetes   bmi smoker
#>     <int> <int>  <int> <dbl>  <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1       0  1151    347  62.9  0.472    0.149  27.4  0.226
#> 2       1   849    282  67.8  0.408    0.335  28.9  0.287


(If you prefer, cohort <- read.csv("cohort.csv") loads exactly the same data from the downloadable CSV file.)
849 patients (42%) were treated, and 629 (31%) died during follow-up. The treated patients are on average about 5 years older, and twice as likely to have diabetes (33% vs 15%). They also died slightly more often (33% vs 30%), even though we know the treatment helps.

title: 5  Confounding and propensity scores
section: 5.3 The naive analysis gets it wrong
text:
5.3 The naive analysis gets it wrong
If we ignore the confounders and just compare treated with untreated patients, the Cox model gets the answer badly wrong:

coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ treated, data = cohort) |>
  broom::tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)

#> # A tibble: 1 x 7
#>   term    estimate std.error statistic p.value conf.low conf.high
#>   <chr>      <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 treated     1.11    0.0802      1.28   0.200    0.947      1.30


The naive HR is about 1.11: treatment looks harmful. Let’s see why by comparing the baseline characteristics of the two groups.
To compare groups on variables measured in different units (years, kg/m², yes/no), we use the standardised mean difference (SMD). It is the difference between the group means, divided by the pooled standard deviation (roughly, the average of the two groups’ standard deviations):
\[
\text{SMD} = \frac{\text{mean in treated} - \text{mean in untreated}}{\text{pooled standard deviation}}
\]
So an SMD of 0.5 means the groups differ by half a standard deviation, whatever the units. Unlike a p-value, it doesn’t depend on the sample size. The bal.tab() function from the cobalt package calculates SMDs (more on cobalt in Section 6.2):

bal.tab(treated ~ age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker,
        data = cohort, s.d.denom = "pooled", binary = "std",
        thresholds = c(m = 0.1))

#> Balance Measures
#>             Type Diff.Un     M.Threshold.Un
#> age      Contin.  0.5101 Not Balanced, >0.1
#> female    Binary -0.1297 Not Balanced, >0.1
#> diabetes  Binary  0.4451 Not Balanced, >0.1
#> bmi      Contin.  0.3454 Not Balanced, >0.1
#> smoker    Binary  0.1412 Not Balanced, >0.1
#> 
#> Balance tally for mean differences
#>                    count
#> Balanced, <0.1         0
#> Not Balanced, >0.1     5
#> 
#> Variable with the greatest mean difference
#>  Variable Diff.Un     M.Threshold.Un
#>       age  0.5101 Not Balanced, >0.1
#> 
#> Sample sizes
#>     Control Treated
#> All    1151     849








TipHow to read this output




Type: whether each variable is continuous or binary (yes/no).
Diff.Un: the SMD in the unmatched data. A positive value means the treated group has a higher mean, or for binary variables a higher proportion.
M.Threshold: whether the |SMD| is below 0.1 (“Balanced”) or not.



An |SMD| above 0.1 is a common rule of thumb for meaningful imbalance. Age (SMD 0.51) and diabetes (0.45) are strongly imbalanced, and BMI, smoking and sex are imbalanced too.

title: 5  Confounding and propensity scores
section: 5.4 Why not just adjust in a Cox model?
text:
5.4 Why not just adjust in a Cox model?
You already know one way to deal with confounders: put them in the Cox model, as in Chapter 3. That is a perfectly good approach, and Chapter 7 compares it with matching. So why learn another one? Propensity score methods have four practical advantages:

Design before outcomes. Matching and checking balance use only the baseline variables and who was treated. You settle the comparison groups before seeing any survival results, as you would when designing a trial, so you can’t (even unconsciously) pick the analysis that gives the answer you hoped for.
You can see whether the groups are comparable. Balance tables and overlap plots show exactly where treated and untreated patients don’t resemble each other. A Cox model will compare them anyway, without warning, by extrapolating from patients who aren’t really comparable.
Many confounders, few events. A Cox model needs roughly 10–20 deaths for each coefficient (Chapter 3). The propensity score model’s outcome is treatment, which is usually far more common than death, so it can include many confounders. The survival model after matching then needs only one coefficient, for treatment.
A clear target. Matching estimates the effect in a well-defined group of patients, those who were treated (see the box on estimands later in this chapter).

They have costs too. Matching usually discards some patients, which costs precision. And neither approach can deal with confounders that weren’t measured. In practice the two are often used together, as you’ll see in Chapter 7.

title: 5  Confounding and propensity scores
text:
5.5 The propensity score

5.5.1 The idea
We have five confounders. To compare like with like, we could try to match every treated patient with an untreated patient of the same age, sex, diabetes status, BMI and smoking status. With only five variables that’s already hard. Exact matches on age and BMI are rare. With twenty variables it’s impossible.
The propensity score (often shortened to PS) gets around this by combining all the confounders into a single number: each patient’s probability of being treated, given their covariates:
\[
e(x) = \Pr(\text{Treated} = 1 \mid X = x)
\]
A patient with a propensity score of 0.8 had characteristics that made treatment very likely. A patient with a score of 0.1 was unlikely to be treated. Whether each patient was actually treated is a separate question.
Rosenbaum and Rubin (1983) showed that the propensity score is a balancing score. Among patients with the same propensity score, the measured covariates have the same distribution in the treated and untreated groups. Consider two patients who both had a 60% chance of treatment. One got it and one didn’t. They are comparable as far as the measured covariates are concerned. So instead of matching on five (or fifty) variables at once, we can match on one number.






ImportantThe big assumption: no unmeasured confounding



Propensity scores can only balance the confounders you measured and included. Unlike randomisation, they do nothing about unmeasured ones (frailty, disease severity not in the records, and so on). The app later in this chapter lets you see this happen. Choosing covariates needs subject-matter knowledge, not just statistics.




5.5.2 Worked example: estimating the propensity score
We don’t know the true probability of treatment, so we estimate it. The usual method is a logistic regression with treatment as the outcome and the confounders as predictors. The survival outcome plays no part here: this model only describes who gets treated.

ps_model <- glm(treated ~ age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker,
                data = cohort, family = binomial)

# Odds ratios: how each characteristic changes the odds of being treated
broom::tidy(ps_model, exponentiate = TRUE)

#> # A tibble: 6 x 5
#>   term        estimate std.error statistic  p.value
#>   <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 (Intercept)  0.00149   0.494      -13.2  1.20e-39
#> 2 age          1.05      0.00531      9.99 1.64e-23
#> 3 female       0.735     0.0985      -3.13 1.74e- 3
#> 4 diabetes     2.71      0.117        8.55 1.22e-17
#> 5 bmi          1.09      0.0110       8.18 2.93e-16
#> 6 smoker       1.53      0.112        3.82 1.31e- 4


The estimate column holds the odds ratios (exponentiate = TRUE converts the coefficients to odds ratios, as it did for hazard ratios in Chapter 3). They show the confounding by indication we built in. Each extra year of age raises the odds of treatment by about 5%, and diabetes nearly triples them. Each patient’s fitted probability from this model is their estimated propensity score:

cohort$ps       <- fitted(ps_model)       # propensity score (a probability)
cohort$logit_ps <- qlogis(cohort$ps)      # the same score on the log-odds scale

cohort |>
  select(id, age, female, diabetes, bmi, smoker, treated, ps) |>
  head()

#>   id age female diabetes  bmi smoker treated        ps
#> 1  1  70      1        0 33.6      0       0 0.4792373
#> 2  2  54      0        0 26.5      0       0 0.2205669
#> 3  3  66      1        0 36.4      0       0 0.4890299
#> 4  4  64      0        0 20.8      0       0 0.2238142
#> 5  5  58      0        1 24.5      1       0 0.5487230
#> 6  6  40      0        0 30.3      0       0 0.1591873


A useful first check is how much the two groups’ scores overlap:

ggplot(cohort, aes(ps, fill = factor(treated, labels = c("Untreated", "Treated")))) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5, colour = NA) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#E69F00", "#0072B2")) +
  labs(x = "Estimated propensity score", y = "Density", fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)







Figure 5.1: Estimated propensity scores in treated and untreated patients. Matching is only possible where the two distributions overlap.





Treated patients tend to have higher scores, as expected. But the distributions overlap over most of the range, so most treated patients should have untreated patients with similar scores. Where there is no overlap (here, at the very top end), comparable patients don’t exist, and no method can conjure them up.


5.5.3 Seeing the balancing property
Here’s a direct way to see that the score balances the covariates. Split the patients into five equal-sized groups (quintiles) by propensity score. Then compare treated and untreated patients within each group:

cohort$ps_quintile <- ntile(cohort$ps, 5)      # 1 = lowest fifth of scores, 5 = highest

cohort |>
  group_by(ps_quintile, treated) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_age = mean(age), prop_diabetes = mean(diabetes))

#> # A tibble: 10 x 5
#> # Groups:   ps_quintile [5]
#>    ps_quintile treated     n mean_age prop_diabetes
#>          <int>   <int> <int>    <dbl>         <dbl>
#>  1           1       0   324     55.1        0     
#>  2           1       1    76     55.5        0.0526
#>  3           2       0   266     61.9        0.0301
#>  4           2       1   134     62.0        0.0448
#>  5           3       0   254     65.1        0.154 
#>  6           3       1   146     66.0        0.0959
#>  7           4       0   191     69.1        0.241 
#>  8           4       1   209     68.5        0.268 
#>  9           5       0   116     72.2        0.672 
#> 10           5       1   284     74.2        0.718


Read the table in pairs of rows. Each quintile has one row for untreated patients (treated = 0) and one for treated patients (treated = 1).
Overall, treated patients were about 5 years older (67.8 vs 62.9) and twice as likely to have diabetes. Within each quintile, the differences mostly disappear. In the middle quintile, for example, both groups are aged about 65–66. Each quintile still covers a fairly wide range of scores, so the balance isn’t perfect. Matching goes further, by pairing patients whose scores are very close.


5.5.4 Practice: fill in the blanks
This is a live exercise: edit the code, click Run Code, and your answer is checked automatically. See Section 1.4.1 if you haven’t used one before.
Estimate the propensity scores yourself. The simulated cohort is already loaded. Replace each ______, then click Run Code.


















NoteHint 1





Logistic regression is a glm() with family = binomial. The fitted probabilities come from fitted().











NoteHint 2





tapply(x, group, mean) calculates the mean of x in each group.











TipSolution





ps_model <- glm(treated ~ age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker,
                data = cohort, family = binomial)
cohort$ps <- fitted(ps_model)
tapply(cohort$ps, cohort$treated, mean)
The average propensity score is about 0.37 in untreated patients and 0.50 in treated patients. Treated patients had characteristics that made treatment more likely. That is the confounding by indication the propensity score captures.









5.5.5 Which covariates should go in?

Include pre-treatment variables that affect the outcome, especially if they also affect treatment (true confounders).
Never include variables measured after treatment that could be affected by it (mediators), or the outcome itself.
Variables that predict treatment but not outcome (instruments) don’t help, and they increase variance.
Don’t choose covariates by p-values. Draw a causal diagram (DAG). The website dagitty.net is useful for this.
The aim of the PS model is balance, not prediction. A model that predicts treatment very well is not necessarily a better PS model.

title: 5  Confounding and propensity scores
text:
5.6 Matching on the propensity score

5.6.1 Nearest-neighbour matching, by hand
The simplest and most common approach is 1:1 nearest-neighbour matching:

Take a treated patient.
Find the untreated patient whose propensity score is closest. In matching, untreated patients are usually called controls.
Pair them, and remove that untreated patient from the pool, so that each control is used only once (matching without replacement).
Repeat for the next treated patient.

Distances are usually measured on the logit (log-odds) scale, \(\log\{e/(1-e)\}\), not on the probability scale. On the probability scale, scores are squashed together near 0 and 1, so a difference of 0.02 means much more at \(e = 0.95\) than at \(e = 0.5\). The logit scale spreads them out evenly.
Let’s match four treated patients by hand. To keep it simple, we look for each patient’s nearest control independently, ignoring step 3:


Show the code for this example
controls <- filter(cohort, treated == 0)

nearest_control <- function(lp) {
  i <- which.min(abs(controls$logit_ps - lp))
  tibble(control_id = controls$id[i], control_age = controls$age[i],
         control_diab = controls$diabetes[i], control_ps = controls$ps[i],
         distance = abs(controls$logit_ps[i] - lp))
}

# Three ordinary treated patients, plus the treated patient with the highest score
example <- cohort |>
  filter(treated == 1) |>
  slice(c(1, 2, 3, which.max(ps)))

bind_cols(
  example |> select(id, age, diabetes, ps),
  bind_rows(lapply(example$logit_ps, nearest_control))
) |>
  mutate(across(c(ps, control_ps), \(x) round(x, 3)), distance = round(distance, 3))


#>    id age diabetes    ps control_id control_age control_diab control_ps
#> 1   8  55        1 0.544       1005          76            1      0.545
#> 2   9  66        0 0.441       1486          67            0      0.440
#> 3  13  63        1 0.533       1181          61            1      0.533
#> 4 585  93        1 0.938        946          71            1      0.863
#>   distance
#> 1    0.005
#> 2    0.001
#> 3    0.001
#> 4    0.867


Each row is one treated patient (id, age, diabetes, ps), next to the untreated patient with the closest score (control_…). distance is how far apart their scores are on the logit scale.
The first three treated patients each find a control with an almost identical score, and similar characteristics. The last patient is different. Their score is about 0.94, and the closest untreated patient scores only about 0.86, a long way off on the logit scale. Is that pair really comparable? This is what a caliper is for.


5.6.2 The caliper
A caliper is the maximum distance allowed between the scores of two matched patients. If a treated patient has no control within the caliper, they are left unmatched and dropped from the analysis, rather than being paired with a poor match.
The usual choice is 0.2 standard deviations of the logit propensity score (Austin 2011b):

caliper <- 0.2 * sd(cohort$logit_ps)
caliper

#> [1] 0.1692203


In this cohort the caliper is about 0.17 on the logit scale. The first three pairs above are well inside it. The fourth (distance ≈ 0.88) is far outside it, so that patient would be dropped.
Calipers involve a trade-off:









Wider caliper (or none)
Narrower caliper




Balance
Worse: poor matches allowed
Better: only close matches


Patients kept
More
Fewer, as more treated patients are dropped


Who the result applies to
Close to all treated patients
Only the treated patients who have comparable controls



That last row matters. Dropped patients are usually the ones with the most extreme scores, the most “obviously treat” cases. After matching, the estimate applies to the remaining, more typical treated patients. Always report how many were dropped.






NoteEstimands: who is the effect for?



Matching each treated patient to a control builds a sample that looks like the treated group. So it estimates the:

ATT: average effect of treatment in the treated. “For the kind of patients who get this drug, what did it do?”

An alternative is the:

ATE: average effect if everyone in the population were treated vs if no-one were. Weighting methods (IPTW) or full matching can target the ATE (see Chapter 9).

With a caliper, the estimate applies to the matched treated patients.

title: 5  Confounding and propensity scores
text:
5.8 Summary






ImportantKey points




A confounder affects both who gets treated and the outcome. Ignoring confounders can reverse the direction of an effect. Here, a naive HR of 1.11 hid a real benefit.
SMDs measure imbalance on a common scale. |SMD| > 0.1 is a common sign of meaningful imbalance.
The propensity score is the probability of treatment given the measured covariates. It is estimated by logistic regression. Patients with similar scores have similar covariates, so matching on one number balances them all.
Nearest-neighbour matching pairs each treated patient with the untreated patient (the control) whose logit propensity score is closest. A caliper (usually 0.2 SD) stops poor matches. Treated patients with no close match are dropped, so the result applies to the matched treated patients (the ATT).
Matching only balances measured confounders. It can’t fix confounders you didn’t measure.



Answering the question. The treated patients were sicker to begin with: older, more often diabetic, with higher BMI and more often smokers. Their average propensity score was 0.50, compared with 0.37 for untreated patients. Matching on the propensity score can create comparable groups. Chapter 6 does the matching in R and checks that it worked, and Chapter 7 then compares survival.

title: 6  Matching in R
text:
6.2 The workflow, and the tools
Putting it all together, a propensity score analysis has six steps:

Specify the confounders and the estimand.
Estimate the propensity score, usually by logistic regression.
Match treated to untreated patients with similar scores.
Check balance in the matched sample. If it’s poor, go back to step 2 or 3, e.g. add interactions or squared terms, or change the caliper. Don’t look at outcomes until the design is settled.
Estimate the treatment effect in the matched sample (Chapter 7).
Think about sensitivity to unmeasured confounding.

In Chapter 5 we did steps 2 and 3 by hand, to see how they work. In practice, you use two R packages:

MatchIt (Ho et al. 2011) does steps 2 and 3 in one function, matchit(). It fits the propensity score model, then matches using the method, ratio and caliper you choose. It returns the matched data, ready for analysis.
cobalt does step 4. It produces balance tables (bal.tab()) and plots, including the Love plot (love.plot()), which shows the SMD of each covariate before and after matching.

section: 6.3 Propensity score matching in R with MatchIt
text:
6.3 Propensity score matching in R with MatchIt

6.3.1 Steps 2–3: estimate the PS and match
matchit() does what we did by hand in Chapter 5 (Section 5.5 and Section 5.6). It fits the same logistic regression, then performs 1:1 nearest-neighbour matching without replacement, with a caliper of 0.2 SDs of the logit propensity score:

m_out <- matchit(
  treated ~ age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker,  # the PS model
  data     = cohort,
  method   = "nearest",      # greedy nearest-neighbour matching
  distance = "glm",          # propensity score from logistic regression ...
  link     = "linear.logit", # ... with distances on the logit scale
  caliper  = 0.2,            # max distance: 0.2 SDs of the logit PS
  ratio    = 1               # 1 control per treated patient
)
m_out

#> A matchit object
#>  - method: 1:1 nearest neighbor matching without replacement
#>  - distance: Propensity score [caliper]
#>              - estimated with logistic regression and linearized
#>  - caliper: <distance> (0.169)
#>  - number of obs.: 2000 (original), 1428 (matched)
#>  - target estimand: ATT
#>  - covariates: age, female, diabetes, bmi, smoker








TipHow to read this output



A summary of what was done: the matching method, how the propensity score was estimated (“linearized” means the logit scale), the caliper (0.169), and the number of patients before (2000) and after (1428) matching.
Watch the scale. The caliper of 0.169 matches the value we calculated by hand in Chapter 5, because link = "linear.logit" puts it on the logit scale (Austin 2011). Without that argument, matchit() measures distances and the caliper on the probability scale.




6.3.2 Step 4: check balance with summary() and cobalt

summary(m_out, un = FALSE)   # un = FALSE hides the pre-matching table

#> 
#> Call:
#> matchit(formula = treated ~ age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker, 
#>     data = cohort, method = "nearest", distance = "glm", link = "linear.logit", 
#>     caliper = 0.2, ratio = 1)
#> 
#> Summary of Balance for Matched Data:
#>          Means Treated Means Control Std. Mean Diff. Var. Ratio eCDF Mean
#> distance       -0.1728       -0.2500          0.0936     1.1902    0.0239
#> age            66.4818       65.7983          0.0715     1.0372    0.0142
#> female          0.4300        0.4160          0.0285          .    0.0140
#> diabetes        0.2549        0.2213          0.0712          .    0.0336
#> bmi            28.6483       28.4917          0.0351     0.9791    0.0092
#> smoker          0.2619        0.2675         -0.0124          .    0.0056
#>          eCDF Max Std. Pair Dist.
#> distance   0.0854          0.0941
#> age        0.0700          0.8591
#> female     0.0140          1.0432
#> diabetes   0.0336          0.5284
#> bmi        0.0336          1.0055
#> smoker     0.0056          0.8480
#> 
#> Sample Sizes:
#>           Control Treated
#> All          1151     849
#> Matched       714     714
#> Unmatched     437     135
#> Discarded       0       0








TipHow to read this output



Top table: balance in the matched data, one row per covariate (distance is the propensity score itself).

Means Treated / Means Control: the group means after matching. For binary variables these are proportions.
Std. Mean Diff.: the SMD. This is the column to check: every value should be close to 0 (|SMD| < 0.1).
The other columns (Var. Ratio, eCDF, Std. Pair Dist.) compare other features of the distributions. You can leave them for now.

Sample sizes: All is before matching. Matched is the patients kept. Unmatched is the patients left out, here 135 treated patients with no control within the caliper, plus the spare controls.


Every SMD is below 0.1, so the matching has balanced the measured covariates.
A Love plot shows balance before and after matching at a glance. (It’s named after the statistician Thomas Love, who popularised it, not after the emotion.)

love.plot(m_out, stats = "mean.diffs", abs = TRUE, binary = "std",
          thresholds = c(m = 0.1), var.order = "unadjusted",
          colors = c("#E69F00", "#0072B2"), shapes = c("circle", "triangle"))







Figure 6.1: Covariate balance before and after matching.





Check the overlap of propensity scores, before and after:

bal.plot(m_out, var.name = "distance", which = "both",
         type = "histogram", mirror = TRUE,
         colors = c("#E69F00", "#0072B2"))







Figure 6.2: Distribution of propensity scores before and after matching.





For continuous variables, check the whole distribution, not just the mean:

bal.plot(m_out, var.name = "age", which = "both")







Figure 6.3: Distribution of age in treated and control patients, before and after matching.







6.3.3 Getting the matched data
match.data() returns the matched sample. It has three extra columns: distance (the PS), weights (all 1 for 1:1 matching) and subclass (which pair each patient belongs to). We’ll need subclass for the standard errors in Chapter 7.

matched <- match.data(m_out)
dim(matched)

#> [1] 1428   12

head(matched[, c("id", "treated", "age", "diabetes", "distance", "weights", "subclass")])

#>   id treated age diabetes    distance weights subclass
#> 1  1       0  70        0 -0.08309869       1      374
#> 3  3       0  66        0 -0.04388743       1      576
#> 5  5       0  58        1  0.19551254       1       54
#> 7  7       0  58        0 -0.20062921       1        7
#> 8  8       1  55        1  0.17718583       1      631
#> 9  9       1  66        0 -0.23877486       1      675




6.3.4 Practice: fill in the blanks
This is a live exercise: edit the code, click Run Code, and your answer is checked automatically. See Section 1.4.1 if you haven’t used one before.
The simulated cohort is already loaded. Replace each ______, then click Run Code. (The first run downloads MatchIt and cobalt, so it takes a little longer.)


















NoteHint 1





The logit-scale option is "linear.logit". The caliper and the SMD threshold are numbers from this chapter: 0.2 and 0.1.











NoteHint 2





The function that extracts the matched data is match.data().











TipSolution





m <- matchit(treated ~ age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker,
             data = cohort, method = "nearest",
             link = "linear.logit", caliper = 0.2)
summary(m, un = FALSE)$nn
bal.tab(m, binary = "std", thresholds = c(m = 0.1))
matched <- match.data(m)
nrow(matched)
714 treated patients were matched to 714 controls, so the matched data have 1428 rows. 135 treated patients had no control within the caliper. Every covariate is “Balanced, <0.1” after matching.














NoteGoing further (optional): other matching and weighting options






ratio = 2: up to 2 controls per treated patient. More precise, but balance is sometimes a little worse.
replace = TRUE: controls can be reused. Better balance when good controls are scarce, but you need weights in the analysis.
method = "optimal" or "full": optimal pair matching, or full matching (keeps everyone; can target the ATE). Needs the optmatch package.
exact = ~ female: force exact matches on key variables.
Greedy vs optimal. Greedy matching (the default) takes treated patients one at a time, so early choices can “use up” controls that would suit later patients better. Optimal matching minimises the total distance across all pairs.
Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) with the WeightIt package: no one is discarded, and it targets the ATE by default. Check balance the same way with cobalt.
Use distance = "gbm" or other machine-learning PS models when the treatment model is complicated.

For more, with worked examples of IPTW, matching with replacement, exact and full matching, and how to choose between them, see Chapter 9.

text:
6.4 Exercise

6.4.1 Exercise 6.1
The simulated cohort is already loaded in each box. Each part changes one matching choice and asks what happens. The parts are checked separately.

Part 1: no caliper
This is the matching from this chapter. Remove the caliper, then run it. How many treated patients are matched now, and how does balance compare?


















NoteHint 1





Delete , caliper = 0.2 from the matchit() call (keep the closing bracket).











TipSolution





m_nocal <- matchit(treated ~ age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker,
                   data = cohort, method = "nearest",
                   link = "linear.logit")
summary(m_nocal, un = FALSE)$nn
bal.tab(m_nocal, binary = "std", thresholds = c(m = 0.1))
Without a caliper, all 849 treated patients are matched (there are more controls than treated patients, so everyone finds someone). But the matches for the high-scoring treated patients are poor, and balance is much worse: age (SMD 0.25), diabetes (0.29) and BMI (0.15) are all still above 0.1. Keeping everyone isn’t worth it if the groups aren’t comparable.









Part 2: two controls per treated patient
Keep the caliper, but allow up to 2 controls for each treated patient (see the optional box on other matching options). What happens to the sample size and the balance?


















NoteHint 1





ratio = 2 allows up to two controls per treated patient.











TipSolution





m_r2 <- matchit(treated ~ age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker,
                data = cohort, method = "nearest",
                link = "linear.logit", caliper = 0.2,
                ratio = 2)
summary(m_r2, un = FALSE)$nn
bal.tab(m_r2, binary = "std", thresholds = c(m = 0.1))
The same 714 treated patients are matched, now to 987 controls instead of 714, so the analysis would be more precise. R warns that not every treated patient found 2 controls within the caliper. Every covariate is still balanced (|SMD| below 0.1), though balance is slightly worse than with 1:1 matching: the SMD for age rises to 0.08, and the propensity score itself (distance) is just over the threshold, at 0.12. With a variable number of controls per patient, the matching weights are no longer all 1, so they must be used in the analysis (Chapter 7).









Part 3: leave a confounder out
Remove smoker from the propensity score model. Then check whether smoking is balanced after matching. Because smoker is no longer in the model, bal.tab() needs addl = ~ smoker to include it. Make the balance table the last line.


















NoteHint 1





Delete + smoker from the formula in matchit().











NoteHint 2





Then addl = ~ smoker adds smoking to the balance table.











TipSolution





m_nosmk <- matchit(treated ~ age + female + diabetes + bmi,
                   data = cohort, method = "nearest",
                   link = "linear.logit", caliper = 0.2)
bal.tab(m_nosmk, addl = ~ smoker, binary = "std", un = TRUE)
The four variables in the model are balanced, but smoking isn’t: its SMD is 0.16 after matching, slightly worse than the 0.14 before. Nothing in the matching made smoking balance. Because smoking affects survival, the treatment effect estimate would be confounded. This is the measured version of the unmeasured-confounding problem from Section 5.7.

text:
6.5 Summary






ImportantKey points




matchit() estimates the propensity score and matches in one step. Use link = "linear.logit" so that distances and the caliper are on the logit scale.
The output shows how many patients were matched. Treated patients with no control within the caliper are dropped. Always report how many.
Check balance with summary() or bal.tab(): every |SMD| should be below 0.1. Love plots and distribution plots show the same thing visually.
match.data() returns the matched data, with weights and subclass (the matched pairs), ready for analysis.
Check balance before looking at any outcomes.



Answering the question. matchit() matched 714 treated patients to 714 controls. 135 treated patients had no control within the caliper. After matching, every covariate had |SMD| < 0.1, so the matched groups are comparable on all five measured confounders. Chapter 7 compares their survival.

7.2 Step 2: Kaplan–Meier curves before and after matching


Show the plotting code
p_before <- survfit2(Surv(time, status) ~ treated, data = cohort) |>
  ggsurvfit(linewidth = 1) +
  add_confidence_interval() +
  add_risktable(risktable_stats = "n.risk") +
  scale_ggsurvfit(x_scales = list(breaks = 0:8)) +
  labs(title = "Before matching (confounded)", x = "Years")

p_after <- survfit2(Surv(time, status) ~ treated, data = matched) |>
  ggsurvfit(linewidth = 1) +
  add_confidence_interval() +
  add_risktable(risktable_stats = "n.risk") +
  scale_ggsurvfit(x_scales = list(breaks = 0:8)) +
  labs(title = "After matching", x = "Years")

patchwork::wrap_plots(ggsurvfit_build(p_before), ggsurvfit_build(p_after), ncol = 1)








Figure 7.1: Kaplan–Meier curves by treatment in the full (confounded) cohort and in the propensity-score-matched cohort.





Before matching, the treated group seems to do slightly worse, because they were older and sicker. After matching, the comparison is like for like and the benefit appears.







NoteGoing further (optional): which log-rank test for matched data?





A standard log-rank test on matched data ignores the pairing, and so it is slightly conservative. The Cox model with robust standard errors below is the better test. If you want a pair-respecting log-rank-type test, use coxph(... + strata(subclass)): its score test is a stratified log-rank test.

title: 7  Putting it together: a matched survival analysis
text:
7.3 Step 3: estimate the hazard ratio
In the matched sample we fit a Cox model with treatment only. Two details matter:

weights = weights: these are all 1 here, but they are needed for matching with replacement or with variable ratios. Including them always is a good habit.
robust = TRUE, cluster = subclass: a cluster-robust (sandwich) standard error. This allows for the fact that matched pairs are similar (Austin 2014). It’s called a sandwich because of the shape of its formula: a filling (how much the data actually vary) between two identical slices of “bread” (from the usual, model-based formula).


cox_matched <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ treated,
                     data = matched, weights = weights,
                     robust = TRUE, cluster = subclass)
summary(cox_matched)

#> Call:
#> coxph(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ treated, data = matched, 
#>     weights = weights, robust = TRUE, cluster = subclass)
#> 
#>   n= 1428, number of events= 485 
#> 
#>             coef exp(coef) se(coef) robust se      z Pr(>|z|)    
#> treated -0.38908   0.67768  0.09199   0.08980 -4.333 1.47e-05 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#>         exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95
#> treated    0.6777      1.476    0.5683    0.8081
#> 
#> Concordance= 0.552  (se = 0.012 )
#> Likelihood ratio test= 18.14  on 1 df,   p=2e-05
#> Wald test            = 18.77  on 1 df,   p=1e-05
#> Score (logrank) test = 18.11  on 1 df,   p=2e-05,   Robust = 18.57  p=2e-05
#> 
#>   (Note: the likelihood ratio and score tests assume independence of
#>      observations within a cluster, the Wald and robust score tests do not).








TipHow to read this output



This is read the same way as in Chapter 3. Look at exp(coef) (the HR, 0.68) and its 95% CI (0.57 to 0.81). The new column is robust se, the cluster-robust standard error. R uses it automatically for the CI and p-value.


Check the proportional hazards assumption for this model too:

cox.zph(cox_matched)

#>         chisq df    p
#> treated 0.768  1 0.38
#> GLOBAL  0.768  1 0.38


p = 0.38, so there’s no evidence that the treatment HR changes over follow-up.

7.3.1 Practice: fill in the blanks
This is a live exercise: edit the code, click Run Code, and your answer is checked automatically. See Section 1.4.1 if you haven’t used one before.
The matched data from this chapter, matched, are already loaded. Replace each ______, then click Run Code.


















NoteHint 1





The model contains only the treatment variable, treated. A robust SE needs robust = TRUE.











NoteHint 2





The matched pairs are identified by the subclass column. Time is in years, so 3 years is 3.











TipSolution





cox_m <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ treated, data = matched,
               weights = weights,
               robust = TRUE, cluster = subclass)
summary(cox_m)$conf.int

km_m <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ treated, data = matched)
summary(km_m, times = 3)
Only treated goes in the model: matching has already balanced the confounders, so the model just compares the matched groups. (Adding the covariates as well is the “doubly robust” option in Exercise 7.1.) cluster = subclass tells R which patients form each matched pair. The HR is 0.68 (95% CI 0.57 to 0.81). 3-year survival is about 84% (95% CI 82% to 87%) with treatment and 75% (95% CI 72% to 79%) without.

title: 7  Putting it together: a matched survival analysis
text:
7.4 Step 4: compare the approaches
How does the matched estimate compare with other ways of analysing the same data? We fit four Cox models:

Naive: treatment only, in the full cohort. No adjustment at all.
Covariate-adjusted: treatment plus all five confounders, in the full cohort (the Chapter 3 approach).
PS-matched: treatment only, in the matched cohort (Step 3).
PS-matched + covariates: matching and adjustment together. This is often called doubly robust, because it gives you two chances to get it right: if either the matching or the outcome model deals with the confounding well, the estimate should be close to the truth.



Show the code that fits the four models and builds the table
fits <- list(
  "Naive (unadjusted)" =
    coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ treated, data = cohort),
  "Covariate-adjusted Cox" =
    coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ treated + age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker,
          data = cohort),
  "PS-matched Cox" = cox_matched,
  "PS-matched Cox + covariates" =
    coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ treated + age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker,
          data = matched, weights = weights, robust = TRUE, cluster = subclass)
)

results <- bind_rows(lapply(fits, \(f)
  tidy(f, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |> filter(term == "treated")),
  .id = "method") |>
  select(method, HR = estimate, lower = conf.low, upper = conf.high, p.value) |>
  mutate(n = sapply(fits, \(f) f$n), events = sapply(fits, \(f) f$nevent))

results |> mutate(across(HR:p.value, \(x) signif(x, 3)))


#> # A tibble: 4 x 7
#>   method                         HR lower upper     p.value     n events
#>   <chr>                       <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>       <dbl> <int>  <dbl>
#> 1 Naive (unadjusted)          1.11  0.947 1.3   0.2          2000    629
#> 2 Covariate-adjusted Cox      0.662 0.558 0.787 0.00000266   2000    629
#> 3 PS-matched Cox              0.678 0.568 0.808 0.0000147    1428    485
#> 4 PS-matched Cox + covariates 0.619 0.515 0.744 0.000000301  1428    485


Each row gives the HR for treatment from one method, with its CI, p-value, and the number of patients and deaths used.


Show the plotting code
results |>
  mutate(method = factor(method, levels = rev(method))) |>
  ggplot(aes(HR, method)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.70, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#D55E00") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.73, linetype = "dotted", colour = "#CC79A7", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper), width = 0.15, orientation = "y") +
  geom_point(size = 3, colour = "#0072B2") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.70, y = 4.45, label = "conditional", colour = "#D55E00", hjust = 1.05) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.73, y = 4.45, label = "marginal", colour = "#CC79A7", hjust = -0.05) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 1, 1.2)) +
  labs(x = "Hazard ratio for treatment (log scale)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








Figure 7.2: Estimated treatment hazard ratios by method. The dashed line marks the true conditional HR (0.70), and the dotted line the true marginal HR in the treated (0.73).





The naive analysis gets the direction wrong. Both covariate adjustment and PS matching come close to the truth. Notice, though, that there are two “truths” on the plot, because the methods answer slightly different questions:

The covariate-adjusted Cox model estimates a conditional HR: the effect of treatment for patients with the same age, sex, diabetes, BMI and smoking status. Its true value is 0.70, the number we built into the data.
The PS-matched Cox model, with only treated, estimates a marginal HR: the effect of treatment on average, across the kind of patients who were treated. Its true value here is about 0.73.

Hazard ratios have an odd property: even with no confounding at all, the average effect over a mixed group of patients is a little closer to 1 than the effect for any particular kind of patient. (This is called non-collapsibility.) Neither number is wrong. They answer different questions, so say which one you estimated (Austin 2014). The matched estimate (0.68) is well within sampling error of its truth (0.73).
Notice that the table shows only the HR for treatment. The covariate-adjusted models also give HRs for age, diabetes, BMI and so on, and it’s tempting to report and interpret those too. Don’t. Those variables are in the model to remove confounding of the treatment effect, and their own HRs don’t mean what they seem to. For example, in this cohort older patients are more likely to have diabetes, which is one of the ways age affects survival. The HR for age is adjusted for diabetes, so it leaves that pathway out: it isn’t “the effect of age”. Interpreting every HR in the model as an effect is known as the Table 2 fallacy (Westreich and Greenland 2013). The name comes from the usual layout of a paper: Table 1 describes the patients, and Table 2 reports the model, where every coefficient sits side by side as if they all meant the same thing. If you want the effect of another variable, it needs its own analysis, with its own confounders.







NoteGoing further (optional): where does 0.73 come from?





The true marginal HR in the treated isn’t written into the simulation, so we work it out by brute force. Simulate a very large cohort, and give every treated patient two survival times: one with treatment and one without, using the same random number for both. Comparing the two sets of times gives the true average effect of treatment in the treated, with the same follow-up as in the real study:

big <- simulate_cohort(n = 200000, seed = 1)
tr  <- big[big$treated == 1, ]
n_t <- nrow(tr)

# Each treated patient's risk score, from the model in simulate_cohort()
lp <- with(tr, 0.06 * (age - 65) + 0.6 * diabetes + 0.03 * (bmi - 28) -
               0.25 * female + 0.55 * smoker)

# Two survival times per patient: without and with treatment (HR 0.70)
set.seed(1)
u <- runif(n_t)
t_untreated <- (-log(u) / (0.05 * exp(lp)))^(1 / 1.2)
t_treated   <- (-log(u) / (0.05 * exp(lp + log(0.70))))^(1 / 1.2)

# The same censoring as in the study
t_cens <- pmin(runif(n_t, 3, 8), rexp(n_t, rate = 0.04))

both <- data.frame(
  time   = c(pmin(t_untreated, t_cens), pmin(t_treated, t_cens)),
  status = c(t_untreated <= t_cens, t_treated <= t_cens),
  trt    = rep(0:1, each = n_t)
)
exp(coef(coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ trt, data = both)))

#>       trt 
#> 0.7324347


The answer depends a little on how long patients are followed: with no censoring at all, it would be about 0.77.

text:
7.5 Step 5: absolute effects are easier to explain
HRs are relative. Clinicians and patients often find absolute survival differences easier to understand, e.g. “5-year survival was 69% with treatment and 61% without”. You can read these straight off the matched KM curves, using summary() as in Chapter 2:

km_m <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ treated, data = matched)
s5 <- summary(km_m, times = 5)

# The key numbers, one row per group
data.frame(group    = s5$strata,
           survival = round(s5$surv, 3),
           lower    = round(s5$lower, 3),
           upper    = round(s5$upper, 3))

#>       group survival lower upper
#> 1 treated=0    0.609 0.570  0.65
#> 2 treated=1    0.690 0.651  0.73


summary() returns a list, and here we pick out the parts we need: the estimated 5-year survival in each group (treated=0 and treated=1), with the lower and upper limits of its 95% CI. Printing s5 itself shows the same numbers, plus the number at risk and the number of deaths.







NoteGoing further (optional): restricted mean survival time (RMST)





The restricted mean survival time is the average event-free time up to a chosen horizon, e.g. “on average, treated patients lived 4.3 of the first 5 years”. It doesn’t rely on proportional hazards, so it is useful when that assumption fails:

print(km_m, rmean = 5)   # RMST up to 5 years, by group

#> Call: survfit(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ treated, data = matched)
#> 
#>             n events rmean* se(rmean) median 0.95LCL 0.95UCL
#> treated=0 714    280   3.98    0.0590   6.42    5.77      NA
#> treated=1 714    205   4.30    0.0512     NA    7.64      NA
#>     * restricted mean with upper limit =  5


The rmean column is the RMST in each group.
For more, including how to compare two groups’ RMSTs with a confidence interval and how to choose the time horizon, see Chapter 10.

title: 7  Putting it together: a matched survival analysis
text:
7.6 Step 6: sensitivity to unmeasured confounding
Matching can’t fix confounders you didn’t measure (try the “Severity unmeasured” scenario in Section 5.7 again). So always ask: is there an important confounder we didn’t measure? Discuss it honestly in the limitations.







NoteGoing further (optional): the E-value





The E-value (VanderWeele and Ding 2017) asks how strong an unmeasured confounder would need to be to explain away the result. The EValue package calculates it:
# install.packages("EValue")
EValue::evalues.HR(est = 0.68, lo = 0.57, hi = 0.81, rare = FALSE)

text:
7.8 Exercise

7.8.1 Exercise 7.1
A new cohort, null_cohort, is loaded in each box. It was made with simulate_cohort(n = 5000, hr_treat = 1, seed = 1), so the true effect is null (HR = 1). The exercise has three parts, each checked separately. The first run downloads some packages and matches 5000 patients, so it may take a little while.

Part 1: naive and matched analyses
Fit the naive Cox model. Then match the patients, and fit the matched Cox model (make that the last line). What do the two analyses conclude?


















NoteHint 1





Use the same caliper as before (0.2), and extract the matched data with match.data().











NoteHint 2





The matched pairs are identified by subclass.











TipSolution





coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ treated, data = null_cohort)
m_null <- matchit(treated ~ age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker,
                  data = null_cohort, link = "linear.logit", caliper = 0.2)
md_null <- match.data(m_null)
coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ treated, data = md_null,
      robust = TRUE, cluster = subclass)
The naive analysis is badly wrong: HR ≈ 1.86. A treatment that does nothing looks like it nearly doubles the hazard of death. Matching removes most of that bias, bringing the HR down to about 1.21. But it doesn’t get all the way to 1: the CI (1.09–1.34) still excludes the null. Parts 2 and 3 look at why.









Part 2: balance and KM curves
The matched data, md_null, are ready in this box. Draw matched KM curves, then check balance (make the balance table the last line). Are any covariates still slightly imbalanced?


















NoteHint 1





The usual threshold for |SMD| is 0.1.











TipSolution





survfit2(Surv(time, status) ~ treated, data = md_null) |>
  ggsurvfit() +
  add_risktable() +
  labs(x = "Years")
bal.tab(m_null, binary = "std", thresholds = c(m = 0.1))
All the SMDs are below 0.1, so by the usual rule of thumb the matching “passed”. But small imbalances remain (age ≈ 0.06, diabetes ≈ 0.07). These are strong predictors of death, so even small imbalances leave some residual confounding. Chance plays a part too: a fully adjusted Cox model on the whole cohort also gives about 1.09.









Part 3: doubly robust
Refit the matched Cox model with the five covariates added (“doubly robust”). What changes?


















NoteHint 1





Add age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker after treated.











TipSolution





coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ treated + age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker,
      data = md_null, robust = TRUE, cluster = subclass)
Adding the covariates mops up much of the remaining confounding: HR ≈ 1.12, CI 1.00–1.25. Combining matching with adjustment like this is called doubly robust estimation: the matching and the outcome model each get a chance to deal with the confounding, so what one misses, the other can catch.
The lesson: matching reduces confounding but rarely eliminates it. For strong prognostic variables, aim for SMDs well below 0.1, and consider covariate adjustment in the matched sample as well.

title: 7  Putting it together: a matched survival analysis
text:
7.9 Summary






ImportantKey points




Design first, outcomes second: settle the matching and check balance before looking at survival.
In the matched sample, fit a Cox model with treatment only, using the matching weights and a robust (cluster) standard error for the matched pairs.
Here, matching turned a misleading naive HR of 1.11 into 0.68, close to the true marginal HR of 0.73. Full covariate adjustment gave an answer close to the true conditional HR of 0.70. The two truths differ because the methods answer slightly different questions.
Report absolute effects too, such as survival at 5 years, which are easier to explain than HRs.
Matching reduces confounding but rarely removes it completely, and it can’t fix unmeasured confounders. Say so in the limitations.



Answering the question. Yes. In the matched cohort the hazard ratio was 0.68 (95% CI 0.57 to 0.81), about a 32% lower hazard of death with treatment. Estimated 5-year survival was 69% with treatment and 61% without.

8.2 App 1: survival explorer
Download survival-explorer.R
Three real datasets from the survival package: lung, veteran (a randomised lung cancer trial) and colon (an adjuvant chemotherapy trial).

Kaplan–Meier tab. Choose a grouping variable. Toggle confidence intervals, risk tables and the median. Shows the log-rank test.

PH check tab. cox.zph() tests and Schoenfeld residual plots.







TipSuggested activities




In veteran, compare the treatment groups by KM. Then fit a Cox model with treatment, celltype and karno. Check PH. karno clearly violates it. What would you do? (Hint: Section 3.6.)

veteran. The KM curves for the two treatments cross and the log-rank test is far from significant (\(\chi^2 = 0.008\)). In the Cox model, the Test treatment HR is about 1.30, not significant. cox.zph() flags karno (p < 0.001) and celltype (p ≈ 0.002). The effect of performance status is strong early on and fades over time. Options are strata(celltype) and a time-varying effect for karno, e.g. split follow-up with survSplit() or use tt(karno).
colon. Without adjustment, Lev+5FU vs observation has HR ≈ 0.69 (95% CI 0.55–0.87), and levamisole alone has HR ≈ 0.97. Adjusting for nodes and differ barely changes this (HR ≈ 0.67), as you’d expect in a randomised trial. Adjustment can improve precision, but it shouldn’t move the estimate much. 8.3 App 2: propensity score explorer
Download psm-explorer.R
Simulates the observational cohort from Chapters 5–7, with adjustable sample size, true HR and strength of confounding. You can then:

choose which confounders go into the PS model (leave one out to create an unmeasured confounder);
choose 1:k nearest-neighbour matching (ratio, replacement, caliper) or inverse probability weighting;
see balance (Love plot and PS distributions) for all true confounders, matched or weighted KM curves, and a comparison of HRs from the naive analysis, full covariate adjustment and the PS method, against the truth.







TipSuggested activities




Set confounding to 3. Compare 1:1 matching with no caliper, 1:1 with a 0.2 caliper, and IPTW. Look at balance, sample size (or effective sample size) and the HR.
Untick age. Age is the strongest confounder, so balance on age collapses and every PS estimate is biased.
Set the true HR to 1 and confounding to 2. How wrong is the naive analysis?









NoteAnswers





With the default seed (2026), true HR 0.7:

Confounding = 3. The naive HR is about 1.75. With 1:1 matching and no caliper, every treated patient is matched, but the |SMD| for age is still about 1.0. The matched HR is about 1.65, barely better than the naive one. With the 0.2 caliper, only 468 of 972 treated patients are kept. Balance is much better, though age is still just over the threshold (SMD ≈ 0.11). The HR is about 0.83, still a bit biased. IPTW also gives about 0.83, but the largest weight is about 60 and the effective sample size falls to roughly a third. When the groups barely overlap, every method struggles. Full covariate adjustment (0.74) does best here because the outcome model is correctly specified, which you can never guarantee in real data.
Untick age (confounding = 1). Age is no longer balanced, and the matched HR jumps to about 0.98, so the benefit disappears completely.
True HR = 1, confounding = 2. The naive HR is about 2.0, which looks like a doubling of risk from a treatment that does nothing. The matched estimate is about 1.02, close to the truth.

title: 9  Weighting and other matching methods
text:
9.1 Weighting instead of matching
Matching makes the treated and untreated groups comparable by choosing patients. Weighting does it by counting some patients more than others.
Think about a patient with a propensity score of 0.2: someone like them had only a 20% chance of being treated. Out of 100 such patients, about 20 would be treated and 80 not. If we want a comparison as if treatment had been decided at random, the 20 treated patients are under-represented. Giving each of them a weight of \(1/0.2 = 5\) lets them stand for all 100. The 80 untreated patients each get a weight of \(1/(1 - 0.2) = 1.25\), which also adds up to 100.
Do this for everyone, and both groups end up looking like the whole population. In this weighted pseudo-population, treatment is no longer related to the measured confounders, just as in a randomised trial. This is inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW): each patient is weighted by the inverse (one divided by) of the probability of the treatment they actually received.
The weights depend on whose effect you want (the estimand, Section 5.6):
Here \(e\) is the patient’s propensity score. ATT weights leave the treated patients as they are, and reweight the untreated patients to look like them. That’s the same target as 1:1 matching, but nobody is discarded.
