text:
9.2 Worked example: IPTW in the simulated cohort
We use the same simulated cohort as in Chapters 5–7 (Section 5.2), and the same propensity score model:

ps_model <- glm(treated ~ age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker,
                data = cohort, family = binomial)
cohort$ps <- fitted(ps_model)

# ATE weights: 1/e for treated patients, 1/(1 - e) for untreated patients
cohort$w_ate <- ifelse(cohort$treated == 1,
                       1 / cohort$ps,
                       1 / (1 - cohort$ps))

summary(cohort$w_ate)

#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>   1.067   1.377   1.684   1.999   2.253  11.676



9.2.1 Step 1: look at the weights
The weights range from about 1.1 to 11.7. The largest weight belongs to this patient:

cohort[which.max(cohort$w_ate), c("age", "female", "diabetes", "bmi",
                                  "smoker", "treated", "ps", "w_ate")]

#>    age female diabetes  bmi smoker treated         ps    w_ate
#> 15  40      1        0 25.9      0       1 0.08564543 11.67605


A 40-year-old non-smoking woman without diabetes had only a 9% chance of being treated, but was treated. She stands in for about 12 patients like her, most of whom weren’t treated. A few large weights are normal. But when a handful of patients carry very large weights, the results depend heavily on them, and the estimate becomes imprecise.
A useful summary is the effective sample size (ESS): roughly, how many equally weighted patients the weighted sample is worth. bal.tab() reports it in the next step. Here, the 849 treated patients are worth about 673 after weighting, which is fine. An ESS that is much smaller than the group size is a warning sign.


9.2.2 Step 2: check balance
bal.tab() checks balance in the weighted sample, just as it did after matching:

bal.tab(treated ~ age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker,
        data = cohort, weights = "w_ate",
        s.d.denom = "pooled", binary = "std",
        thresholds = c(m = 0.1))

#> Balance Measures
#>             Type Diff.Adj    M.Threshold
#> age      Contin.  -0.0001 Balanced, <0.1
#> female    Binary  -0.0229 Balanced, <0.1
#> diabetes  Binary   0.0096 Balanced, <0.1
#> bmi      Contin.  -0.0083 Balanced, <0.1
#> smoker    Binary   0.0005 Balanced, <0.1
#> 
#> Balance tally for mean differences
#>                    count
#> Balanced, <0.1         5
#> Not Balanced, >0.1     0
#> 
#> Variable with the greatest mean difference
#>  Variable Diff.Adj    M.Threshold
#>    female  -0.0229 Balanced, <0.1
#> 
#> Effective sample sizes
#>            Control Treated
#> Unadjusted 1151.    849.  
#> Adjusted    993.62  672.66








TipHow to read this output




Diff.Adj: the SMD in the weighted data. Every value should be close to 0 (|SMD| < 0.1).
Effective sample sizes: the size of each group before (Unadjusted) and after (Adjusted) weighting.



Every SMD is now very close to zero, and every patient has been kept.


9.2.3 Step 3: weighted KM curves
survfit() and survfit2() accept a weights argument. The weighted KM curves estimate what survival would have been if everyone had been treated, and if no-one had:

survfit2(Surv(time, status) ~ treated, data = cohort, weights = w_ate) |>
  ggsurvfit(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_ggsurvfit(x_scales = list(breaks = 0:8)) +
  labs(x = "Years")







Figure 9.1: IPTW-weighted Kaplan–Meier curves (ATE weights).







9.2.4 Step 4: weighted Cox model

cox_ate <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ treated, data = cohort,
                 weights = w_ate, robust = TRUE)
summary(cox_ate)$conf.int

#>         exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95
#> treated 0.6964938   1.435763 0.5855802 0.8284152


With weights, you need a robust (sandwich) standard error. An ordinary standard error would treat a weight of 5 as five real patients, and the confidence interval would be far too narrow. Recent versions of the survival package use a robust standard error automatically when the weights aren’t all 0 or 1, but writing robust = TRUE makes it explicit, and protects you in older versions and in other software.
The HR is 0.70 (95% CI 0.59 to 0.83). Like the matched model in Chapter 7, this is a marginal HR, but now for the whole population rather than for the treated. Its true value, worked out by the same brute-force simulation as in Chapter 7, is about 0.73, well within the confidence interval.
ATT weights give an estimate for the same target as 1:1 matching:

cohort$w_att <- ifelse(cohort$treated == 1,
                       1,
                       cohort$ps / (1 - cohort$ps))

coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ treated, data = cohort,
      weights = w_att, robust = TRUE) |>
  broom::tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

#> # A tibble: 1 x 4
#>   term    estimate conf.low conf.high
#>   <chr>      <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 treated    0.701    0.590     0.832


HR 0.70 (95% CI 0.59 to 0.83), compared with 0.68 from matching, but now without dropping the 135 treated patients who had no match.


9.2.5 Practice: ATT weights
This is a live exercise: edit the code, click Run Code, and your answer is checked automatically. See Section 1.4.1 if you haven’t used one before.
The simulated cohort is loaded, with each patient’s propensity score in ps. Calculate ATT weights, check balance, and fit the weighted Cox model. Replace each ______, then click Run Code.


















NoteHint 1





Treated patients get a weight of 1. For untreated patients, the denominator is 1 - cohort$ps.











NoteHint 2





With weights, always use robust = TRUE.











TipSolution





cohort$w_att <- ifelse(cohort$treated == 1,
                       1,
                       cohort$ps / (1 - cohort$ps))
bal.tab(treated ~ age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker,
        data = cohort, weights = "w_att", binary = "std",
        thresholds = c(m = 0.1))
cox_att <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ treated, data = cohort,
                 weights = w_att, robust = TRUE)
summary(cox_att)$conf.int
Every covariate is balanced after weighting. The HR is 0.70 (95% CI 0.59 to 0.83), close to the 0.68 from 1:1 matching, but using all 2000 patients rather than 1428.

9.3 Extreme weights: stabilising and trimming
IPTW has a weak spot. A treated patient with a propensity score of 0.01 gets a weight of 100. A few patients like that can dominate the analysis. Large weights are a sign of poor overlap: patients who were almost certain to get (or not get) treatment, with hardly anyone comparable in the other group. Two common remedies:

Stabilised weights. Multiply each weight by the overall proportion of patients who got the treatment they received. The weights then average about 1 and add up to about the real sample size. The HR doesn’t change, but the weights are easier to inspect.
Excluding patients with extreme scores (for example, propensity scores below 0.05 or above 0.95). This removes the patients who have no comparable counterparts, but it changes who the result applies to, so say who was excluded.
Capping (truncating) the weights, for example at their 99th percentile. Everyone is kept and the estimate is more stable, but the capped weights may no longer balance the groups, which can bring back bias. The app below shows how badly this can go wrong.

Whichever you do, check balance again afterwards, and report the range of the weights or the ESS alongside an IPTW analysis.

9.5 In practice: the WeightIt package
Calculating weights by hand shows how they work. In practice, the WeightIt package does it for you, with the same interface as MatchIt, and cobalt checks balance directly:

W <- weightit(treated ~ age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker,
              data = cohort, method = "glm", estimand = "ATE")
summary(W)

#>                   Summary of weights

#> - Weight ranges:

#> treated 1.0665 |---------------------------| 11.6760
#> control 1.0823 |---------------|              7.3133

#>  control 5.8899 6.2964 6.5792  6.5924 7.3133
#>

#> treated       0.512 0.356   0.105       0
#> control       0.398 0.258   0.063       0
#> 
#> - Effective Sample Sizes:
#> 
#>            Control Treated

#> Weighted    993.62  672.66



bal.tab(W, binary = "std", thresholds = c(m = 0.1))

#> Balance Measures
#>                Type Diff.Adj    M.Threshold
#> prop.score Distance   0.0040 Balanced, <0.1
#> age         Contin.  -0.0001 Balanced, <0.1

#>            Control Treated
#> Unadjusted 1151.    849.  
#> Adjusted    993.62  672.66

coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ treated, data = cohort,
      weights = W$weights, robust = TRUE) |>
  broom::tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

#> # A tibble: 1 x 4

9.6 Other kinds of matching
Chapter 6 used 1:1 nearest-neighbour matching without replacement, with a caliper. MatchIt offers several variations. Here are the ones you’re most likely to meet.

9.6.1 Matching with replacement
With replace = TRUE, each control can be matched to more than one treated patient. Good controls are no longer “used up”, so more treated patients find a close match:

m_rep <- matchit(treated ~ age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker,
                 data = cohort, method = "nearest",
                 link = "linear.logit", caliper = 0.2,
                 replace = TRUE)
summary(m_rep, un = FALSE)$nn

#>                 Control Treated
#> All (ESS)     1151.0000     849
#> All           1151.0000     849
#> Matched (ESS)  282.4489     844
#> Matched        466.0000     844
#> Unmatched      685.0000       5
#> Discarded        0.0000       0


Now 844 of the 849 treated patients are matched, but to only 466 different controls. Some controls are used several times, so the matching weights are no longer all 1. Check balance, then use the weights in the analysis:

bal.tab(m_rep, binary = "std", thresholds = c(m = 0.1))

#> Balance Measures
#>              Type Diff.Adj        M.Threshold
#> distance Distance   0.0006     Balanced, <0.1
#> age       Contin.   0.0739     Balanced, <0.1
#> female     Binary   0.0121     Balanced, <0.1
#> diabetes   Binary  -0.0075     Balanced, <0.1
#> bmi       Contin.  -0.1181 Not Balanced, >0.1
#> smoker     Binary   0.0812     Balanced, <0.1
#> 
#> Balance tally for mean differences
#>                    count
#> Balanced, <0.1         5
#> Not Balanced, >0.1     1
#> 
#> Variable with the greatest mean difference
#>  Variable Diff.Adj        M.Threshold
#>       bmi  -0.1181 Not Balanced, >0.1
#> 
#> Sample sizes
#>                      Control Treated
#> All                  1151.       849
#> Matched (ESS)         282.45     844
#> Matched (Unweighted)  466.       844
#> Unmatched             685.         5

md_rep <- match.data(m_rep)
summary(md_rep$weights[md_rep$treated == 0])

#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>  0.5521  0.5521  0.5521  1.0000  1.1043  6.6256

coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ treated, data = md_rep,
      weights = weights, robust = TRUE) |>
  broom::tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

#> # A tibble: 1 x 4
#>   term    estimate conf.low conf.high
#>   <chr>      <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 treated    0.669    0.541     0.827


The cost is precision: the 466 controls, unevenly weighted, are worth only about 280 equally weighted patients (the ESS in the matching summary). Balance can also suffer when the same few controls are reused. Here, BMI ends up just over the threshold (SMD 0.12).


9.6.2 Exact matching on key variables
exact = ~ diabetes only allows matches between patients with the same diabetes status, while still matching on the propensity score within that group. It’s useful for one or two variables that must match exactly, for example sex in a sex-specific outcome, or study site:

m_ex <- matchit(treated ~ age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker,
                data = cohort, method = "nearest",
                link = "linear.logit", caliper = 0.2,
                exact = ~ diabetes)
summary(m_ex, un = FALSE)$nn

#>               Control Treated
#> All (ESS)        1151     849
#> All              1151     849
#> Matched (ESS)     706     706
#> Matched           706     706
#> Unmatched         445     143
#> Discarded           0       0


Here 706 treated patients are matched, a few fewer than without the exact condition (714).


9.6.3 Optimal and full matching
Both need the optmatch package (install.packages("optmatch")).

Optimal pair matching (method = "optimal"). Nearest-neighbour matching is greedy: it takes treated patients one at a time, so an early match can use up a control that would have suited a later patient better. Optimal matching chooses all the pairs together, to minimise the total distance. Results are usually similar to nearest-neighbour matching.
Full matching (method = "full"). Every patient is placed in a matched set containing at least one treated and one untreated patient. A set might have one treated patient and five controls, or three treated patients and one control. Nobody is discarded, and with weights it can target the ATE or the ATT. It often gives the best balance of all the matching methods.

m_full <- matchit(treated ~ age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker,
                  data = cohort, method = "full",
                  link = "linear.logit", estimand = "ATE")
The analysis afterwards is the same as for matching with replacement: use the weights, with a robust standard error clustered on subclass.

9.8 Summary






ImportantKey points




IPTW weights each patient by one over the probability of the treatment they received, creating a pseudo-population in which treatment is unrelated to the measured confounders. Nobody is discarded.
ATE weights (\(1/e\), \(1/(1-e)\)) target the whole population. ATT weights (1, \(e/(1-e)\)) target the treated, like 1:1 matching.
Check the weights (range, ESS) and the balance, use the weights in KM curves and Cox models, and always use robust standard errors.
Very large weights signal poor overlap. Stabilise or trim them, and report what you did.
MatchIt also offers matching with replacement, exact matching, and optimal and full matching. Most of these need the matching weights in the analysis.
Choose a main method in advance, and use another as a sensitivity analysis.



Answering the question. Yes. Weighting uses every patient. In the simulated cohort, IPTW gave an HR of 0.70 for the whole population (true marginal value about 0.73), and ATT weights gave 0.70 for the treated, close to the 0.68 from matching, without discarding the 135 unmatched treated patients.

title: 10  When proportional hazards fail
text:
10.1 First: does it matter?
Chapter 3 showed how to check the proportional hazards assumption. Before changing your analysis, ask two questions.
Which variable fails? If it’s a covariate you’re only adjusting for, stratify on it: each level gets its own baseline hazard, the variable gets no HR, and the HRs you care about are unaffected (Exercise 3.1 did this for ECOG). If a continuous covariate fails, split it into groups and stratify, or use the methods below. Problems with the main exposure need more thought, because they change what you can report.
How badly does it fail? With a lot of data, cox.zph() can flag tiny, unimportant changes. Always look at the plot. If the line is roughly flat, with small wiggles, a single HR is a fair summary. If it clearly changes direction or size, a single HR misleads.

title: 10  When proportional hazards fail
text:
10.2 A treatment whose effect reverses
Here’s a simulated trial where it matters. 800 patients are randomised to surgery or medical treatment. Surgery carries early risks: for the first 6 months the hazard of death is twice as high. After that, it’s half as high. (The code is folded away; open it if you’re interested.)


Show the simulation code
set.seed(2027)
n <- 800
surgery <- rep(0:1, each = n / 2)          # 400 medical (0), 400 surgery (1)
u  <- runif(n)
h0 <- 0.4                                   # medical: constant hazard, 0.4 per year

# Surgery: twice the hazard for 6 months, then half the hazard
t_medical <- -log(u) / h0
t_surgery <- ifelse(-log(u) < 2 * h0 * 0.5,
                    -log(u) / (2 * h0),
                    0.5 + (-log(u) - 2 * h0 * 0.5) / (0.5 * h0))

t_event <- ifelse(surgery == 1, t_surgery, t_medical)
t_cens  <- runif(n, 2, 5)                   # follow-up ends 2-5 years after entry

trial <- data.frame(
  surgery = surgery,
  time    = pmin(t_event, t_cens),
  status  = as.numeric(t_event <= t_cens)
)



survfit2(Surv(time, status) ~ surgery, data = trial) |>
  ggsurvfit(linewidth = 1) +
  add_risktable(risktable_stats = "n.risk") +
  scale_ggsurvfit() +
  labs(x = "Years")







Figure 10.1: Kaplan–Meier curves for the simulated trial. Surgery does worse at first, then better: the curves cross at about 1.8 years.





The standard analysis:

survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ surgery, data = trial)

#> Call:
#> survdiff(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ surgery, data = trial)
#> 
#>             N Observed Expected (O-E)^2/E (O-E)^2/V
#> surgery=0 400      301      285     0.847      1.73
#> surgery=1 400      260      276     0.877      1.73
#> 
#>  Chisq= 1.7  on 1 degrees of freedom, p= 0.2

cox_naive <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ surgery, data = trial)
summary(cox_naive)$conf.int

#>         exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95
#> surgery 0.8941873   1.118334 0.7570367  1.056185

cox.zph(cox_naive)

#>         chisq df       p
#> surgery  46.8  1 7.7e-12
#> GLOBAL   46.8  1 7.7e-12


The log-rank test (p = 0.2) and the Cox model (HR 0.89, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.06) both say “no clear difference”. That’s badly misleading: surgery doubles the early hazard and halves the later one. The two effects cancel out in a single number. cox.zph() flags the problem strongly (p < 0.001). Here are the alternatives.

title: 10  When proportional hazards fail
section: 10.3 Option 1: a separate HR for each period
text:
10.3 Option 1: a separate HR for each period
You met this in Section 3.6. Split follow-up at a time chosen from the plot, or from clinical knowledge, and estimate an HR for each period:

trial_split <- survSplit(Surv(time, status) ~ ., data = trial,
                         cut = 0.5, episode = "period")
trial_split$period <- factor(trial_split$period, levels = 1:2,
                             labels = c("first 6 months",
                                        "after 6 months"))

cox_period <- coxph(Surv(tstart, time, status) ~ surgery:period,
                    data = trial_split)
summary(cox_period)$conf.int

#>                              exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95
#> surgery:periodfirst 6 months 2.2063576  0.4532357 1.6518444 2.9470172
#> surgery:periodafter 6 months 0.5245366  1.9064448 0.4211291 0.6533356


In the first 6 months, surgery more than doubles the hazard (HR 2.21, 95% CI 1.65 to 2.95). After 6 months it halves it (HR 0.52, 0.42 to 0.65). Those are close to the true values we built in (2 and 0.5), and cox.zph(cox_period) shows no remaining problem. This is easy to explain, but it needs a sensible cut point, chosen before looking at p-values.

10.3.1 Practice: a separate HR for each period
This is a live exercise: edit the code, click Run Code, and your answer is checked automatically. See Section 1.4.1 if you haven’t used one before.
The simulated surgery trial is loaded. Split follow-up at 1 year instead of 6 months, and estimate the surgery HR in each period. Replace each ______, then click Run Code.


















NoteHint 1





Time is in years, so 1 year is cut = 1.











NoteHint 2





After splitting, each row runs from tstart to time: Surv(tstart, time, status).

trial_split <- survSplit(Surv(time, status) ~ ., data = trial,
                         cut = 1, episode = "period")
trial_split$period <- factor(trial_split$period, levels = 1:2,
                             labels = c("first year", "after 1 year"))

With the split at 1 year, the first period mixes the harmful first 6 months with 6 months of benefit, so its HR is smaller (about 1.4) than the true early HR of 2. The HR after 1 year (about 0.5) matches the true later effect. A cut point in the wrong place blurs the picture, which is why it should come from the plot or from clinical knowledge.

title: 10  When proportional hazards fail
section: 10.4 Option 2: an HR that changes smoothly over time
text:
10.4 Option 2: an HR that changes smoothly over time
Sometimes an effect fades gradually rather than switching at one moment. The tt() (“time transform”) argument in coxph() lets the log-HR change with time, for example in proportion to log(time).
The real veteran lung cancer trial is a classic example. The Karnofsky performance score strongly predicts survival, but cox.zph() shows its effect changes:

vet <- survival::veteran
cox.zph(coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ trt + karno, data = vet))

#>         chisq df       p
#> trt     0.307  1 0.57942
#> karno  11.959  1 0.00054
#> GLOBAL 13.577  2 0.00113


So we let the Karnofsky effect change with log(time):

cox_tt <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ trt + karno + tt(karno),
                data = vet,
                tt = function(x, t, ...) x * log(t))
summary(cox_tt)$coefficients

#>                  coef exp(coef)    se(coef)          z     Pr(>|z|)
#> trt        0.02893722 1.0293600 0.189420215  0.1527673 8.785818e-01
#> karno     -0.08314604 0.9202167 0.017168667 -4.8428945 1.279612e-06
#> tt(karno)  0.01323575 1.0133237 0.004337927  3.0511697 2.279517e-03








TipHow to read this output




karno and tt(karno) together describe the effect of the score. The log-HR per point at time \(t\) is karno + tt(karno) × log(\(t\)).
tt(karno) is positive (p = 0.002), so the protective effect of a higher score gets weaker as time goes on.



The numbers are hard to read on their own, so calculate the HR at a few times, per 10 points of the score:

b <- coef(cox_tt)
days <- c(7, 30, 90, 180, 365)
hr_10 <- exp(10 * (b["karno"] + b["tt(karno)"] * log(days)))
data.frame(days = days, hr_per_10_points = round(hr_10, 2))

#>   days hr_per_10_points
#> 1    7             0.56
#> 2   30             0.68
#> 3   90             0.79
#> 4  180             0.87
#> 5  365             0.95


A 10-point higher score goes with a 44% lower hazard in the first week (HR 0.56), but only a 5% lower hazard at a year (HR 0.95). That’s the same story as ph.karno in Chapter 3: a doctor’s rating of how well a patient is now predicts the near future much better than the distant future.
The functional form (here log time) is a choice you make, so check it against the cox.zph() plot. The survival package’s guide to time-dependent covariates (Therneau et al., n.d.) covers tt() in more detail.

title: 10  When proportional hazards fail
section: 10.5 Option 3: the restricted mean survival time
text:
10.5 Option 3: the restricted mean survival time
The restricted mean survival time (RMST) avoids hazards altogether. It is the average survival time up to a chosen time horizon, \(\tau\) (“tau”). For example, “over the first 2 years, patients survived for 1.40 years on average”. It equals the area under the KM curve up to \(\tau\):


Show the plotting code
km_trial <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ surgery, data = trial)

# Survival on a fine grid of times up to 2 years, for shading
grid <- summary(km_trial, times = seq(0, 2, by = 0.005), extend = TRUE)
stairs <- data.frame(
  time = grid$time,
  surv = grid$surv,
  arm  = ifelse(grid$strata == "surgery=1", "Surgery", "Medical")
)

ggplot(stairs, aes(time, surv, fill = arm, colour = arm)) +
  geom_area(alpha = 0.25, position = "identity") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ arm) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#E69F00", "#0072B2")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#E69F00", "#0072B2")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 2), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Years", y = "Survival probability") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")








Figure 10.2: The RMST up to 2 years is the shaded area under each KM curve. The difference in RMST is the difference between the two areas.





The survRM2 package compares two groups’ RMSTs:

rmst_2y <- rmst2(time = trial$time, status = trial$status,
                 arm = trial$surgery, tau = 2)
rmst_2y

#> 
#> The truncation time: tau = 2  was specified. 
#> 
#> Restricted Mean Survival Time (RMST) by arm 
#>               Est.    se lower .95 upper .95
#> RMST (arm=1) 1.256 0.041     1.176     1.336
#> RMST (arm=0) 1.404 0.035     1.336     1.472
#> 
#> 
#> Restricted Mean Time Lost (RMTL) by arm 
#>               Est.    se lower .95 upper .95
#> RMTL (arm=1) 0.744 0.041     0.664     0.824
#> RMTL (arm=0) 0.596 0.035     0.528     0.664
#> 
#> 
#> Between-group contrast 
#>                        Est. lower .95 upper .95     p
#> RMST (arm=1)-(arm=0) -0.148    -0.252    -0.043 0.006
#> RMST (arm=1)/(arm=0)  0.895     0.826     0.969 0.006
#> RMTL (arm=1)/(arm=0)  1.248     1.068     1.459 0.005








TipHow to read this output




RMST for each arm (arm=1 is surgery, arm=0 medical): the average survival time, in years, over the first 2 years, with a 95% CI.
RMST (arm=1)-(arm=0): the difference. This is usually the number to report.
The ratio of RMSTs, and the RMTL rows (restricted mean time lost), are other ways of summarising the same thing.



Over the first 2 years, surgery patients survived on average 0.15 years (about 54 days) less than medical patients (95% CI 0.04 to 0.25 years less). But the answer depends on the horizon you choose:

By 4 years, the later benefit of surgery has exactly made up for the early losses. All three answers are correct: they answer different questions. That’s why \(\tau\) must be chosen in advance, for a clinical reason (the length of time that matters to patients, or the follow-up most patients completed), and not picked afterwards to give the most interesting result.

10.5.1 Interactive app: choosing the time horizon
In this app you move \(\tau\) and watch the RMSTs change. With the default settings, it uses exactly the trial above, so the numbers match the table. Changing the effect settings, or the seed, simulates a new trial. The bottom plot shows the RMST difference for every possible \(\tau\), with your choice marked.


import {simSwitch, rmst} from "./js/extras.js"
import {kmFit} from "./js/survtools.js"
formGrid = inputs => html`<div class="form-grid">${Object.values(inputs)}</div>`























viewof rmScen = Inputs.radio(["Default", "No early harm (HR 0.5 throughout)", "Smaller late benefit (HR 0.8)", "Early harm lasts a year"], {value: "Default", label: "Scenario"})
rmP = ({"Default": {}, "No early harm (HR 0.5 throughout)": {"early": 0.5}, "Smaller late benefit (HR 0.8)": {"late": 0.8}, "Early harm lasts a year": {"cut": 1}})[rmScen]
viewof rm = Inputs.form({
  tau:   Inputs.range([0.25, 4.5], {value: rmP.tau ?? 2, step: 0.25, label: "Time horizon τ (years)"}),
  early: Inputs.range([0.3, 3], {value: rmP.early ?? 2, step: 0.1, label: "HR for surgery, early period"}),
  late:  Inputs.range([0.3, 3], {value: rmP.late ?? 0.5, step: 0.1, label: "HR for surgery, later"}),
  cut:   Inputs.range([0.25, 2], {value: rmP.cut ?? 0.5, step: 0.25, label: "Early period lasts (years)"}),
  seed:  Inputs.range([1, 100], {value: rmP.seed ?? 1, step: 1, label: "Random seed (new study)"})
}, {template: formGrid})























rmTrial = FileAttachment("data/surgery_trial.csv").csv({typed: true})
rmIsDefault = rm.early === 2 && rm.late === 0.5 && rm.cut === 0.5 && rm.seed === 1
rmData = rmIsDefault
  ? rmTrial.map(d => ({arm: d.surgery, time: d.time, status: d.status}))
  : simSwitch({n: 800, h0: 0.4, hrEarly: rm.early, hrLate: rm.late, cut: rm.cut, seed: rm.seed})
rmFits = [0, 1].map(a => kmFit(rmData.filter(d => d.arm === a).map(d => d.time), rmData.filter(d => d.arm === a).map(d => d.status)))
rmCurve = {
  const out = [];
  for (let t = 0.25; t <= 4.5001; t += 0.05) out.push({tau: t, diff: rmst(rmFits[1], t) - rmst(rmFits[0], t)});
  return out;
}





































{
  const r0 = rmst(rmFits[0], rm.tau), r1 = rmst(rmFits[1], rm.tau), d = r1 - r0;
  const shade = [];
  for (const [a, lab] of [[0, "Medical"], [1, "Surgery"]]) {
    let s = 1, j = 0; const f = rmFits[a];
    for (let t = 0; t <= rm.tau + 1e-9; t += rm.tau / 300) {
      while (j < f.length && f[j].time <= t) { s = f[j].surv; j++; }
      shade.push({time: t, surv: s, arm: lab});
    }
  }
  const lines = rmFits.flatMap((f, a) => f.filter(r => r.time <= 4.5).map(r => ({...r, arm: a ? "Surgery" : "Medical"})));
  const top = Plot.plot({
    height: 280, y: {domain: [0, 1], grid: true, label: "Survival probability"}, x: {label: "Years →", domain: [0, 4.5]},
    color: {legend: true, domain: ["Medical", "Surgery"], range: ["#E69F00", "#0072B2"]},
    marks: [
      Plot.areaY(shade, {x: "time", y1: 0, y2: "surv", fill: "arm", fillOpacity: 0.15, curve: "step-after"}),
      Plot.line(lines, {x: "time", y: "surv", stroke: "arm", strokeWidth: 2, curve: "step-after"}),
      Plot.ruleX([rm.tau], {stroke: "#333", strokeDasharray: "4,3"})
    ]
  });
  const bottom = Plot.plot({
    height: 200, x: {label: "Time horizon τ (years) →", domain: [0, 4.5]}, y: {label: "RMST difference (years)", grid: true},
    marks: [
      Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: "#888"}),
      Plot.line(rmCurve, {x: "tau", y: "diff", stroke: "#333", strokeWidth: 2}),
      Plot.dot([{tau: rm.tau, diff: d}], {x: "tau", y: "diff", fill: d < 0 ? "#D55E00" : "#009E73", r: 6})
    ]
  });
  const sign = v => (v >= 0 ? "+" : "−") + Math.abs(v).toFixed(2);
  return html`<div>${top}
  <div class="estimates">
  <div class="est"><span>RMST, medical (to ${rm.tau} y)</span><b>${r0.toFixed(2)} y</b><small> </small></div>
  <div class="est"><span>RMST, surgery (to ${rm.tau} y)</span><b>${r1.toFixed(2)} y</b><small> </small></div>
  <div class="est ${d < 0 ? "bad" : "good"}"><span>Difference (surgery − medical)</span><b>${sign(d)} y</b><small>about ${Math.round(Math.abs(d) * 365)} days ${d < 0 ? "less" : "more"}</small></div>
  </div>${bottom}</div>`;
}













TipThings to try



For each one, predict first, then pick the scenario and check.

On the Default scenario, move \(\tau\) from 0.5 to 4.5 years. Predict: at what horizon does surgery stop looking worse?
Predict: what does the bottom plot look like if surgery has no early harm? Then pick No early harm (HR 0.5 throughout).
Predict: if the later benefit is smaller, will surgery ever catch up within 4.5 years? Then pick Smaller late benefit (HR 0.8), and then Early harm lasts a year.









NoteAnswers: what you should see






The difference starts negative (surgery patients lose time early: −0.11 years at 1 year and −0.15 at 2 years), shrinks (−0.09 at 3 years), and crosses zero at 4 years. By 4.5 years surgery is ahead (+0.07). The shaded areas show why: the early gap in the curves is eventually outweighed by the later one. This is why τ must be chosen in advance.
The difference is positive at every horizon, and grows steadily (+0.25 years at 2 years, +0.72 at 4). When hazards are proportional, the RMST and the HR tell the same story, and the choice of τ only changes the size of the benefit, not its direction.
No. With a later HR of 0.8, surgery never catches up within 4.5 years (−0.22 years at 4 years). If the early harm lasts a year, it doesn’t either (−0.34 at 4 years). Whether surgery is “worth it” depends on how big and how long-lasting each effect is, and on the time horizon that matters to patients.

Over the first 3 years, surgery patients survived on average 1.69 years, and medical patients 1.78 years: a difference of −0.09 years (95% CI −0.25 to 0.07). By 3 years the later benefit has made up most of the early losses, so the difference is small and not significant, between the 1- and 4-year results in the table above.

text:
10.6 Option 4: survival at fixed times
The simplest absolute measure, from Chapter 2, also works whatever the hazards do:

km_trial <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ surgery, data = trial)
s <- summary(km_trial, times = c(0.5, 4))
data.frame(arm = s$strata, years = s$time, survival = round(s$surv, 2))

#>         arm years survival
#> 1 surgery=0   0.5     0.83
#> 2 surgery=0   4.0     0.20
#> 3 surgery=1   0.5     0.66
#> 4 surgery=1   4.0     0.31


At 6 months, 83% of medical patients but only 66% of surgery patients were alive. At 4 years, it’s 20% versus 31%. Reporting both, alongside the KM curves, tells the story clearly.

title: 10  When proportional hazards fail
text:
10.7 Option 5: accelerated failure time models
A different kind of regression model describes effects on survival time rather than on the hazard. An accelerated failure time (AFT) model estimates a time ratio: how many times longer (or shorter) one group’s survival times are. survreg() in the survival package fits them. Here it is for sex in the lung data from Chapters 1–3:

lung <- survival::lung
lung$status <- lung$status - 1
lung$sex <- factor(lung$sex, levels = 1:2, labels = c("Male", "Female"))

aft <- survreg(Surv(time, status) ~ sex, data = lung, dist = "weibull")
exp(coef(aft))[2]          # time ratio, women vs men

#> sexFemale 
#>  1.485242

exp(confint(aft))[2, ]     # its 95% CI

#>    2.5 %   97.5 % 
#> 1.156491 1.907447


Women’s survival times are about 1.49 times as long as men’s (95% CI 1.16 to 1.91). Many people find “women lived about 50% longer” easier to grasp than “women had a 41% lower hazard”.
AFT models make their own assumption: that the time ratio is the same throughout follow-up, and that survival times follow the chosen distribution (here Weibull). So they’re an alternative effect measure, not a cure for crossing curves like those in the surgery trial.

Suggested approach

A separate HR for each period

tt(), checked against the cox.zph() plot

Whatever you choose, show the KM curves: they tell the reader what is happening, whichever summary you report alongside them.

title: 10  When proportional hazards fail
text:
10.9 Summary






ImportantKey points




If only a covariate fails PH, stratify on it. Problems with the main exposure change what you should report.
A single HR can hide opposite effects at different times, as in the surgery trial (HR 0.89 overall, but 2.2 early and 0.5 later).
A separate HR for each period (survSplit()) is easy to explain. tt() lets an effect change smoothly with time.
The RMST is the average survival time up to a horizon τ, the area under the KM curve. It doesn’t rely on PH, but its answer depends on τ, so choose τ in advance.
Survival at fixed times and the KM curves themselves always help.
AFT models describe effects as time ratios, with their own assumptions.



Answering the question. Report what the data show over time: the KM curves, survival at clinically important times, and either period-specific HRs or the RMST at a horizon chosen in advance. In the surgery trial, these reveal early harm and later benefit, which the single HR of 0.89 hid completely.

title: 11  Missing data
text:
11.1 What R does by default
Most R modelling functions, including coxph(), quietly drop every row with a missing value in any variable in the model. This is called a complete-case analysis. In the lung data, a few variables have gaps:
colSums(is.na(survival::lung))

#>      inst      time    status       age       sex   ph.ecog  ph.karno pat.karno 
#>         1         0         0         0         0         1         1         3 
#>  meal.cal   wt.loss 
#>        47        14
Each gap looks small. But put several of these variables in one model:
coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ sex + age + ph.ecog + wt.loss + meal.cal,
      data = survival::lung)

#> Call:
#> coxph(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ sex + age + ph.ecog + wt.loss + 
#>     meal.cal, data = survival::lung)
#> 
#>                coef  exp(coef)   se(coef)      z        p
#> sex      -5.400e-01  5.827e-01  1.988e-01 -2.716 0.006602
#> age       8.693e-03  1.009e+00  1.124e-02  0.773 0.439303
#> ph.ecog   5.152e-01  1.674e+00  1.483e-01  3.474 0.000513
#> wt.loss  -1.117e-02  9.889e-01  7.548e-03 -1.480 0.138841
#> meal.cal -4.499e-05  1.000e+00  2.512e-04 -0.179 0.857865
#> 
#> Likelihood ratio test=22.34  on 5 df, p=0.0004517
#> n= 170, number of events= 123 
#>    (58 observations deleted due to missingness)
The last line of the output says it: 58 of the 228 patients (25%) were dropped, and 42 of the 165 deaths. That costs precision, and, as the rest of this chapter shows, it can also bias the results. Always check n and number of events against the size of your data.

m$n

title: 11  Missing data
section: 11.2 When does missing data cause bias?
text:
11.2 When does missing data cause bias?
It depends on why the values are missing. There are three kinds:









Kind
Meaning
Example
Complete-case analysis




MCAR: missing completely at random
Whether a value is missing has nothing to do with the patient
A sample was lost in the post
Unbiased, but wastes data


MAR: missing at random
Whether a value is missing depends on things you have recorded
BMI is recorded less often for patients who died, and you know who died
Can be biased. Multiple imputation can fix it


MNAR: missing not at random
Whether a value is missing depends on the missing value itself, or on things you haven’t recorded
Heavier patients avoid being weighed
Biased, and no standard method fully fixes it



The names are confusing: “missing at random” doesn’t mean the values are missing randomly. It means they’re missing at random once you take account of the recorded information.
For a Cox model, one rule of thumb helps. If whether a covariate is missing depends on the outcome (death, or how long patients survived), a complete-case analysis is usually biased. If it depends only on other covariates in the model, a complete-case analysis is usually fine, just less precise.

title: 11  Missing data
section: 11.3 A demonstration with a known truth
text:
11.3 A demonstration with a known truth
We take the simulated cohort from Chapters 5–7 and delete some BMI values. BMI is recorded less often for patients who died (perhaps their final records were incomplete) and for treated patients (perhaps they were managed at a different clinic):

set.seed(1)
p_miss <- plogis(-1.5 + 1.5 * cohort$status + 1 * cohort$treated)
cohort_miss <- cohort
cohort_miss$bmi[runif(nrow(cohort)) < p_miss] <- NA

mean(is.na(cohort_miss$bmi))                              # overall

#> [1] 0.381

tapply(is.na(cohort_miss$bmi), cohort_miss$status, mean)  # by death

#>         0         1 
#> 0.2735230 0.6152623

tapply(is.na(cohort_miss$bmi), cohort_miss$treated, mean) # by treatment

#>         0         1 
#> 0.2971329 0.4946996


38% of BMI values are now missing: 62% among patients who died, and 49% among treated patients. This is MAR: the chance of being missing depends on things we have recorded.
Compare the covariate-adjusted Cox model fitted to the full data, before anything was deleted, with the complete-case analysis:

covs <- "treated + age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker"
f <- as.formula(paste("Surv(time, status) ~", covs))

full_fit <- coxph(f, data = cohort)        # before deleting anything
cc_fit   <- coxph(f, data = cohort_miss)   # complete cases only

c(full = exp(coef(full_fit))[["treated"]],
  complete_case = exp(coef(cc_fit))[["treated"]])

#>          full complete_case 
#>     0.6622329     0.5018850

cc_fit$n

#> [1] 1238


With the full data, the treatment HR is 0.66 (the truth, which we built into the data, is 0.70). The complete-case analysis uses only 1238 patients and gives 0.50, badly exaggerating the benefit. The patients it keeps are not representative: treated patients who died are the most likely to have been dropped.

title: 11  Missing data
text:
11.4 Multiple imputation
Multiple imputation fills in each missing value with a plausible value, predicted from the patient’s other information, plus some random variation to reflect our uncertainty. It does this several times, making several complete datasets that differ only in the filled-in values. Then:

Impute: create \(m\) completed datasets (often 10 to 50).
Analyse: fit the same model to each one.
Pool: combine the \(m\) results with Rubin’s rules. The pooled estimate is the average of the \(m\) estimates. Its standard error combines the uncertainty within each analysis with the variation between the imputed datasets, so the CI honestly reflects that some values were guessed.

The mice package does all three.

11.4.1 Step 1: include the outcome, the right way
The imputation model must include everything in the analysis model, including the outcome. It feels like cheating to use the outcome to fill in a covariate, but leaving it out biases the results towards no effect.
For survival data, don’t use the raw follow-up time. Instead, include the event indicator (status) and the Nelson–Aalen estimate of the cumulative hazard at each patient’s follow-up time (White and Royston 2009). mice calculates it with nelsonaalen():

cohort_miss$H <- nelsonaalen(cohort_miss, time, status)

# The variables used for imputation: the analysis variables, status and H
imp_data <- cohort_miss[, c("age", "female", "diabetes", "bmi", "smoker",
                            "treated", "status", "H", "time")]

# Keep time in the data (the Cox model needs it), but don't use it to impute
pred <- make.predictorMatrix(imp_data)
pred[, "time"] <- 0



11.4.2 Step 2: impute

imp <- mice(imp_data, m = 10, predictorMatrix = pred,
            seed = 1, printFlag = FALSE)
imp$method

#>      age   female diabetes      bmi   smoker  treated   status        H 
#>       ""       ""       ""    "pmm"       ""       ""       ""       "" 
#>     time 
#>       ""


imp$method shows how each variable is imputed. Only bmi has missing values, and it uses "pmm" (predictive mean matching): each missing BMI is replaced by an observed BMI from a patient with similar predicted values, so the filled-in values are always realistic. seed makes the result reproducible.


11.4.3 Step 3: analyse and pool

fit_mi <- with(imp, coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ treated + age + female +
                            diabetes + bmi + smoker))
pooled <- summary(pool(fit_mi), exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
pooled[, c("term", "estimate", "2.5 %", "97.5 %")]

#>       term  estimate     2.5 %    97.5 %
#> 1  treated 0.6714700 0.5627439 0.8012029
#> 2      age 1.0669140 1.0576171 1.0762925
#> 3   female 0.8032146 0.6839103 0.9433308
#> 4 diabetes 1.7038476 1.4257359 2.0362094
#> 5      bmi 1.0285074 0.9994750 1.0583832
#> 6   smoker 1.7051351 1.4359722 2.0247506








TipHow to read this output




with(imp, coxph(...)) fits the Cox model to each of the 10 completed datasets.
pool() combines them with Rubin’s rules, and summary(..., exponentiate = TRUE) reports hazard ratios.
estimate is the pooled HR, and 2.5 % and 97.5 % its 95% CI.



The pooled HR for treatment is 0.67 (95% CI 0.56 to 0.80), close to the full-data value of 0.66, using all 2000 patients. Multiple imputation has removed the bias that the complete-case analysis introduced.


11.4.4 Practice: multiple imputation
This is a live exercise: edit the code, click Run Code, and your answer is checked automatically. See Section 1.4.1 if you haven’t used one before.
The data with missing BMI values are prepared as in this chapter: imp_data (including status and the Nelson–Aalen estimate H) and the predictor matrix pred. Impute 5 datasets, fit the Cox model to each, and pool the results. The first run downloads the mice package, which can take a minute. Replace each ______, then click Run Code.


















NoteHint 1





m = 5 creates 5 imputed datasets.











NoteHint 2





Rubin’s rules are applied by pool().











TipSolution

            seed = 1, printFlag = FALSE)
fit_mi <- with(imp, coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ treated + age + female +
                            diabetes + bmi + smoker))
summary(pool(fit_mi), exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
With 5 imputations, the pooled HR for treatment is about 0.68, much closer to the full-data value (0.66) than the complete-case estimate (0.50). With more imputations the result would be a little more stable.

title: 11  Missing data
section: 11.5 Missing data and propensity score matching
text:
11.5 Missing data and propensity score matching
Missing confounders cause the same problem for matching: matchit() needs complete data, so the complete cases are matched, with the same bias:

# matchit() needs complete data, so keep only the complete cases
cc_data <- na.omit(cohort_miss[, c("age", "female", "diabetes", "bmi",
                                   "smoker", "treated", "time", "status")])

m_cc <- matchit(treated ~ age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker,
                data = cc_data, method = "nearest",
                link = "linear.logit", caliper = 0.2)
coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ treated, data = match.data(m_cc),
      robust = TRUE, cluster = subclass) |>
  broom::tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

#> # A tibble: 1 x 4
#>   term    estimate conf.low conf.high
#>   <chr>      <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 treated    0.562    0.415     0.760


The MatchThem package matches within each imputed dataset, then pools the results (Pishgar et al. 2021). It works just like matchit(), with datasets = imp in place of data:

mt <- matchthem(treated ~ age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker,
                datasets = imp, approach = "within",
                method = "nearest", link = "linear.logit", caliper = 0.2)

# Balance, summarised across the 10 imputed datasets
bal.tab(mt, binary = "std", thresholds = c(m = 0.1))

#> Balance summary across all imputations
#>              Type Min.Diff.Adj Mean.Diff.Adj Max.Diff.Adj
#> distance Distance       0.0754        0.0843       0.0907
#> age       Contin.       0.0325        0.0510       0.0657
#> female     Binary      -0.0377        0.0014       0.0347
#> diabetes   Binary       0.0299        0.0551       0.0857
#> bmi       Contin.       0.0096        0.0371       0.0598
#> smoker     Binary      -0.0339        0.0063       0.0285
#> 
#> Average sample sizes across imputations
#>              0   1
#> All       1151 849
#> Matched    707 707
#> Unmatched  444 142



fit_mt <- with(mt, coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ treated,
                         weights = weights, robust = TRUE,
                         cluster = subclass))
summary(pool(fit_mt), exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)[
  , c("term", "estimate", "2.5 %", "97.5 %")]

#>      term  estimate     2.5 %    97.5 %
#> 1 treated 0.7470145 0.6162722 0.9054938


The complete-case matched HR is 0.56. After multiple imputation and matching within each dataset, it’s 0.75 (95% CI 0.62 to 0.91), close to the true marginal HR of about 0.73 from Chapter 7.

title: 11  Missing data
text:
11.6 Practical advice

Look before you analyse. Count the missing values in each variable, and compare patients with and without missing data, as for loss to follow-up in Section 4.1.
How many imputations? A common rule of thumb is at least as many as the percentage of incomplete cases (here 38%, so about 40). Ten is fine for learning. Increase \(m\) until the results stop changing.
What to include. Every variable in the analysis model, the outcome (status and the Nelson–Aalen estimate), and any other variables that predict missingness or the missing values.
Report it. Say how much was missing, how you imputed it (method, variables, \(m\)), and compare with the complete-case analysis.
MNAR can’t be fixed by imputation. If values are probably missing for reasons you didn’t record, say so, and consider a sensitivity analysis that shifts the imputed values up or down.
When is complete-case analysis fine? When very little is missing (a few percent), or when missingness depends only on covariates in the model and not on the outcome.

title: 11  Missing data
text:
11.7 Summary






ImportantKey points




R drops incomplete rows by default (complete-case analysis). Always check n and number of events.
Missing data are MCAR, MAR or MNAR. If missingness depends on the outcome, complete-case analysis is usually biased.
Multiple imputation fills in the gaps several times, analyses each completed dataset, and pools the results with Rubin’s rules (mice(), with(), pool()).
Include the outcome in the imputation model: status and the Nelson–Aalen cumulative hazard (nelsonaalen()), not the raw time.
With propensity score matching, impute first, then match within each imputed dataset and pool (MatchThem).
Imputation can’t fix MNAR. Report how much was missing and what you did, and compare with the complete-case analysis.



Answering the question. By default, R analyses only the complete cases. When missingness depends on the outcome, that can be badly biased: in our example, the treatment HR was 0.50 instead of 0.66. Multiple imputation, including the outcome correctly, gave 0.67, and the same idea combined with matching gave 0.75 against a true marginal value of about 0.73.

A.3 Traps: competing risks and time-varying covariates
# Competing risks: event is a factor whose FIRST level is censoring
df$event <- factor(df$event, levels = c("censored", "relapse", "death"))
cif <- survfit(Surv(time, event) ~ group, data = df)   # cumulative incidence
summary(cif, times = 5)                                # Pr(relapse), Pr(death)
coxph(Surv(time, event == "relapse") ~ x, data = df)   # cause-specific Cox
fg <- finegray(Surv(time, event) ~ x, data = df, etype = "relapse")
coxph(Surv(fgstart, fgstop, fgstatus) ~ x, weights = fgwt, data = fg)  # Fine-Gray

# Immortal time: landmark analysis at time L
lm <- subset(df, time > L)                             # alive at the landmark
lm$treated_by_L <- as.numeric(lm$treat_start < L)      # NA start = never treated
survdiff(Surv(time - L, status) ~ treated_by_L, data = lm)

# Immortal time: treatment as a time-varying covariate
tv <- tmerge(df[, c("id", "time", "status")], df, id = id,
             death = event(time, status), treated = tdc(treat_start))
coxph(Surv(tstart, tstop, death) ~ treated, data = tv)

# Non-proportional hazards: a separate HR before and after time c
sp <- survSplit(Surv(time, status) ~ ., data = df, cut = c, episode = "period")
coxph(Surv(tstart, time, status) ~ x:factor(period), data = sp)

title: Appendix B — Glossary
text:
Plain-language definitions of the terms used in this book. The link after each one goes to where it is explained.
Accelerated failure time (AFT) model. A regression model for survival time itself. Its effects are time ratios: a time ratio of 1.5 means survival times are 1.5 times as long. Fitted with survreg(). (Chapter 10)
ATE (average treatment effect). The effect of treatment if everyone in the population were treated, compared with no-one. Weighting (IPTW) or full matching can estimate it. (Section 5.6)
At risk (risk set). The patients who are still being followed and have not yet had the event at a given time. Only they can contribute an event then. (Chapter 2)
ATT (average treatment effect in the treated). The effect of treatment among the kind of patients who actually received it. 1:1 matching of treated to untreated patients estimates the ATT. (Section 5.6)
Balance. Treated and untreated groups are balanced when their covariates have similar distributions. It is usually checked with SMDs. (Section 5.3)
Balancing score. A score such that patients with the same value have the same distribution of measured covariates. The propensity score is one. (Section 5.5)
Caliper. The maximum allowed distance between the propensity scores of two matched patients. Treated patients with no control within the caliper are left unmatched. A common choice is 0.2 standard deviations of the logit propensity score. (Section 5.6.2)
Cause-specific Cox model. A Cox model for one type of event, with competing events treated as censored. It compares the rate of that event among patients still at risk of it. (Section 4.2)
Censoring. When follow-up ends before the event is seen, so we only know that the event happened after a certain time. Administrative censoring: the study ended. Loss to follow-up: the patient left the study. (Chapter 1)
Cohort (observational). A group of people followed over time, where treatment was chosen in routine care rather than by randomisation. (Section 5.2)
Competing risks. Events that prevent the event of interest from happening, e.g. death before relapse. Treating them as censored makes 1 − KM overstate the risk; use the cumulative incidence function instead. (Section 4.2)
Complete-case analysis. Analysing only the patients with no missing values in any variable in the model. It’s R’s default, and can be biased. (Chapter 11)
Confidence interval (95% CI). A range of plausible values for the true quantity, given the data. (Section 1)
Confounder. A variable that affects both who gets a treatment and the outcome. Ignoring confounders can distort or even reverse a treatment effect. Confounding by indication: sicker patients are more likely to be treated. (Chapter 5)
Controls. In matching, the untreated patients who are paired with treated patients. (Section 5.6)
Covariate. A variable included in a model, e.g. age or sex.
Cox model (Cox proportional hazards regression). A regression model for survival data. It estimates hazard ratios for one or more variables without specifying the shape of the baseline hazard. (Chapter 3)
Cumulative incidence function (CIF). The probability of having had a particular event by a given time, allowing for competing events that can happen first. (Section 4.2)
Degrees of freedom (df). Roughly, the number of independent comparisons a test makes. A log-rank test of \(k\) groups has \(k - 1\) df; a test for trend has 1. The df tell R which chi-squared distribution to use for the p-value. (Section 2.6)
Doubly robust. Combining two adjustment methods, e.g. matching and adjusting for the covariates in the matched Cox model. The name means two chances to get it right: the estimate should be close to the truth if either method deals with the confounding well. (Chapter 7)
Effective sample size (ESS). Roughly, how many equally weighted patients a weighted sample is worth. Very unequal weights make it much smaller than the real sample size. (Chapter 9)
Estimand. The precise quantity a study aims to estimate, e.g. the ATT or the ATE. (Section 5.6)
Event. The outcome being timed, e.g. death or relapse. (Chapter 1)
Family-wise error rate (FWER). The chance of at least one false-positive result among a set of tests. Holm and Bonferroni adjustments control it. Compare the false discovery rate (FDR): the expected proportion of significant results that are false positives, which Benjamini–Hochberg controls. (Section 2.6)
Fine–Gray model. A regression model for the cumulative incidence of one type of event when there are competing risks. It compares the probability of the event. (Section 4.2)
Forest plot. A plot showing each estimate (e.g. a hazard ratio) as a point with its confidence interval as a horizontal line, usually on a log scale with a reference line at 1. (Section 3.3.3)
Full matching. A matching method that puts every patient into a matched set with at least one treated and one untreated patient, so nobody is discarded. (Chapter 9)
Hazard. The event rate at a given time among people still at risk: roughly, “the risk right now, given you’ve survived so far”. (Section 2.4.1, Chapter 3)
Hazard ratio (HR). The ratio of two groups’ hazards. HR = 0.6 means the hazard is 40% lower; HR = 1.5 means it is 50% higher. The percentage change is \((\text{HR} - 1) \times 100\%\). (Chapter 3)
Holm adjustment. A way of adjusting p-values when several tests are done, so that the chance of any false-positive result stays at 5%. (Section 2.6)
Immortal time bias. A spurious survival advantage that appears when patients are grouped by something that happens after time zero (e.g. “ever treated”). The group had to survive long enough to get it, so part of their follow-up is time during which they could not die. (Section 4.3)
Informative censoring. Censoring that is related to a patient’s risk, e.g. the sickest patients dropping out. Being censored then tells you something about the patient, and KM estimates are biased. (Section 4.1)
Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW). Weighting each patient by one over the probability of the treatment they received, so that treatment is unrelated to the measured confounders in the weighted sample. (Chapter 9)
Kaplan–Meier (KM) estimator. The standard way to estimate a survival curve from data with censoring. The curve drops at each event time, by the fraction of at-risk patients who had the event. Also called the product-limit estimator. (Chapter 2)
Landmark analysis. Restarting the clock at a chosen time point (the landmark), keeping only patients still followed then, and grouping them by their status at that time. One way to avoid immortal time bias. (Section 4.3)
Logit (log-odds). \(\log\{p/(1-p)\}\). It turns a probability between 0 and 1 into a number on an unlimited scale. Propensity scores are compared on this scale when matching. (Section 1)
Log-rank test. A test of whether two or more survival curves differ. It compares observed with expected numbers of events. (Section 2.4.2)
Love plot. A plot of each covariate’s SMD before and after matching. Named after the statistician Thomas Love, who popularised it. (Chapter 6)
Marginal and conditional hazard ratios. A conditional HR compares patients with the same covariate values (as in an adjusted Cox model). A marginal HR compares the groups on average, across their mix of covariates (as in a matched Cox model with only treated). For hazard ratios the two can differ even without confounding. (Chapter 7)
Matching (nearest-neighbour). Pairing each treated patient with the untreated patient whose propensity score is closest. Without replacement: each control is used only once. (Section 5.6)
MCAR, MAR and MNAR. Missing completely at random (missingness has nothing to do with the patient); missing at random (it depends only on recorded information); missing not at random (it depends on the missing value itself, or on unrecorded information). (Chapter 11)
Median survival. The time by which half the patients have had the event: where the KM curve crosses 0.5. If the curve never gets that low, the median is “not reached”. (Chapter 2)
Multiple imputation. Filling in missing values several times with plausible values, analysing each completed dataset, and combining the results with Rubin’s rules, so the uncertainty about the missing values is reflected in the CI. (Chapter 11)
Nelson–Aalen estimator. An estimate of the cumulative hazard over time. Used to include the survival outcome when imputing missing covariates. (Chapter 11)
Non-informative censoring. The assumption that censored patients have the same future risk as those still being followed. (Chapter 1, Section 4.1)
Odds ratio (OR). The odds of an outcome in one group divided by the odds in another. Logistic regression coefficients are log odds ratios. (Section 1)
Omnibus test. A single test of whether any of several groups differ, e.g. the log-rank test with three or more groups. (Section 2.6)
Overlap (common support). The range of propensity scores where both treated and untreated patients are found. Matching is only possible there. (Figure 5.1)
Power. The chance that a study detects a real effect (gives p < 0.05 when the effect really exists). Small studies, and studies with few events, have low power. (Section 2.5)
Propensity score (PS). A patient’s probability of receiving treatment, given their measured covariates. It is usually estimated by logistic regression. (Section 5.5)
Proportional hazards (PH). The Cox model’s key assumption: the hazard ratio between groups stays constant over time. It is checked with cox.zph(). (Section 3.5)
Reference group. The group that other groups are compared with in a regression model. In R, it’s the first level of a factor. (Section 3.4)
Restricted mean survival time (RMST). The average survival time up to a chosen time horizon: the area under the survival curve up to that time. It doesn’t rely on proportional hazards. (Chapter 10)
Right censoring. The usual kind of censoring: we know only that the event happened after the last follow-up time. (Chapter 1)
Risk table. The table under a KM plot showing how many patients are still at risk at each time. (Chapter 2)
Robust (sandwich) standard error. A standard error that allows for correlated observations, such as members of a matched pair. (Chapter 7)
Schoenfeld residuals. Residuals from a Cox model that show whether a variable’s effect changes over time. cox.zph() tests and plots the scaled Schoenfeld residuals to check proportional hazards. (Section 3.5)
Stabilised weights. IPTW weights multiplied by the overall proportion receiving each treatment, so they average about 1. The HR is unchanged. (Chapter 9)
Standardised mean difference (SMD). The difference between two groups’ means divided by the standard deviation. |SMD| > 0.1 is a common sign of imbalance. (Section 5.3)
Stratification (in a Cox model). Giving each group of a variable its own baseline hazard, using strata(). It is used when that variable breaks the proportional hazards assumption. (Section 3.5)
Survival function, S(t). The probability of being event-free beyond time t. (Chapter 2)
Table 2 fallacy. Interpreting every HR in an adjusted model as an effect, when the model was built to estimate the effect of one variable (e.g. treatment). (Chapter 7)
Test for trend. A test of whether risk changes steadily across ordered groups, e.g. ECOG 0, 1, 2+. (Section 3.4.1)
Time origin. When the clock starts for each patient, e.g. diagnosis or enrolment. (Chapter 1)
Time scale. The units in which time is measured from the origin, e.g. days, years, or age. (Chapter 1)
Time-varying (time-dependent) covariate. A variable whose value can change during follow-up, such as “has had a transplant yet”. Each patient’s follow-up is split into periods, one row per period, and analysed with Surv(start, stop, event). (Section 4.3)
Unmeasured confounding. Confounding by variables that weren’t recorded. No propensity score method can remove it. (Section 5.5)

title: Appendix C — Further reading
text:
C.1 Where to start
Each chapter ends with a short reading list for that chapter. This page collects everything in one place, grouped by topic, with a link to the chapter where each item is most useful. All of it is free to read online unless marked otherwise.
If you read only three things alongside this book, make it these:

title: Appendix C — Further reading
text:
Clark et al. (2003a): survival data, censoring and Kaplan–Meier curves, for clinicians and researchers (Chapters 1–2).
Bradburn et al. (2003a): Cox regression and models with several variables (Chapter 3).
Haukoos and Lewis (2015): a two-page overview of propensity scores and their limits (Chapter 5). (May need institutional access.)

title: Appendix C — Further reading
text:
C.3 The BMJ Statistics Notes
One-page explanations from Martin Bland and Douglas Altman’s long-running series.

Bland and Altman (1998): the Kaplan–Meier method, with a worked example (Chapter 2).
Bland and Altman (2004): how the log-rank test works (Section 2.4.2).

title: Appendix C — Further reading
section: C.4 Hazard ratios and proportional hazards
text:
C.4 Hazard ratios and proportional hazards

Spruance et al. (2004): what a hazard ratio does and doesn’t tell you, and how it relates to probabilities and median survival times (Chapter 3).
Stensrud and Hernán (2020): why hazard ratios often change over time, and why survival curves can be more informative (Section 3.5). (May need institutional access.)
Royston and Parmar (2013): More advanced. The restricted mean survival time, for when hazard ratios aren’t constant (Section 7.5).

title: Appendix C — Further reading
text:
C.5 Common traps

Leung et al. (1997): More advanced. The kinds of censoring, and why the non-informative censoring assumption matters (Section 4.1). (May need institutional access.)
Austin et al. (2016): competing risks: cumulative incidence, cause-specific and Fine–Gray models (Section 4.2).
Suissa (2008): the classic description of immortal time bias, with examples from drug studies (Section 4.3). (May need institutional access.)
Sylvestre et al. (2006): the Oscar-winners reanalysis, a short and memorable example of immortal time bias (Section 4.3).

title: Appendix C — Further reading
text:
C.6 Propensity scores and matching

Austin (2011): the standard introduction to propensity score methods: matching, weighting, stratification and checking balance (Chapter 5).
Stuart (2010): More advanced. A thorough review of matching methods and the choices involved (Chapter 6).
Austin (2014): estimating and reporting treatment effects on survival after propensity score matching, including marginal hazard ratios (Chapter 7).
Westreich and Greenland (2013): the Table 2 fallacy: why the other coefficients in an adjusted model shouldn’t be read as effects (Chapter 7).
VanderWeele and Ding (2017): the E-value, for judging how strong an unmeasured confounder would have to be (Chapter 7).

title: Appendix C — Further reading
section: C.7 Weighting and other matching methods
text:
C.7 Weighting and other matching methods

Chesnaye et al. (2022): a short, clear introduction to inverse probability of treatment weighting (Chapter 9).
Austin and Stuart (2015): best practice for IPTW, including extreme weights and survival outcomes (Chapter 9).

title: Appendix C — Further reading
text:
C.8 When proportional hazards fail

Uno et al. (2014): why and how to report the restricted mean survival time alongside, or instead of, the hazard ratio (Chapter 10).
Royston and Parmar (2013) and Stensrud and Hernán (2020), listed above, are also relevant here.

title: Appendix C — Further reading
text:
C.9 Missing data

Sterne et al. (2009): a readable guide to multiple imputation and its pitfalls (Chapter 11).
White and Royston (2009): how to include a survival outcome when imputing covariates for a Cox model (Chapter 11). (May need institutional access.)
Buuren (2018): a free online book by the author of mice.
Pishgar et al. (2021): matching and weighting after multiple imputation, with the MatchThem package (Chapter 11).

title: Appendix C — Further reading
text:
C.10 Reporting

Elm et al. (2007): the STROBE reporting guideline for observational studies, with a checklist for writing up (Chapter 7).

title: Appendix C — Further reading
text:
C.11 Going deeper

Hernán and Robins (2020): Advanced. A free book on causal inference from observational data: confounding, study design and much more.

The guides written by the packages’ own authors are the best references for the code. Each one can also be opened from R with vignette().

Citing the software
Cite the R packages you use, as well as R itself. Version numbers matter because results and defaults can change between versions. Each package supplies its own reference, and the version printed is the one you have installed:
The grateful package can create a formatted list of package citations for a manuscript automatically: grateful::cite_packages().
